title: The Local Star Formation Environment Predicts Young Star Cluster Radii: Evidence from PHANGS-MUSE H-alpha Maps
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Follow-up to arXiv:2602.00445
summary: The effective radii of young star clusters correlate with cluster mass, but the large scatter about that relation is not well understood. Theory predicts that a cluster's initial radius depends on the gas surface density of its natal environment, so the star formation environment should leave a measurable imprint on cluster structure. In a companion analysis of 5,105 clusters across 31 LEGUS galaxies, we found that galaxy-wide specific star formation rate (sSFR) carries no predictive power for cluster radius. Here we test whether that null result reflects the spatial scale on which the environment was measured. We cross-match the LEGUS cluster catalog of Brown & Gnedin with H-alpha maps from the PHANGS-MUSE survey in the four galaxies common to both surveys, and measure the local star formation rate surface density, Sigma_SFR, at the position of every cluster by aperture photometry. For the 325 clusters younger than 10 Myr with reliable radius and mass measurements, local Sigma_SFR significantly predicts effective radius (beta = 0.079, p = 2 x 10^-4) in a model containing mass and age, while the host galaxy's sSFR does not (beta = 0.042, p = 0.40) for those same clusters. The local model generalizes nearly three times better under cross-validation (CV R^2 = 0.061 versus 0.022). The effect operates among clusters within a single galaxy: it survives galaxy fixed effects (beta = 0.068, p = 0.001) and appears independently in each of the two galaxies large enough to fit alone. Including local Sigma_SFR also reduces the mass coefficient by 26%. The birth environment measurably shapes cluster structure, but only when it is measured on the scale on which clusters actually form.

AI.tldr: Local star formation rate surface density (Sigma_SFR) measurably predicts the effective radii of young (<10 Myr) star clusters, whereas galaxy-wide sSFR does not, indicating that the natal environment shapes cluster structure only when measured on the scale on which clusters form.
AI.motivation: Cluster effective radius correlates with mass, but the large scatter is unexplained. Theory predicts initial cluster radius depends on the gas surface density of the natal environment, so the environment should imprint on cluster structure. A companion analysis found galaxy-wide sSFR has no predictive power for cluster radius; this work tests whether that null result stems from the spatial scale on which environment was measured.
AI.method: Cross-match the LEGUS cluster catalog (Brown & Gnedin) with H-alpha maps from PHANGS-MUSE in the four galaxies common to both surveys. Measure local Sigma_SFR at each cluster position via aperture photometry. Fit models of effective radius using mass, age, and local Sigma_SFR versus host-galaxy sSFR for 325 clusters younger than 10 Myr with reliable radius and mass measurements; assess cross-validated predictive power and robustness with galaxy fixed effects and per-galaxy fits.
AI.result: Local Sigma_SFR significantly predicts effective radius (beta = 0.079, p = 2 x 10^-4) in a model with mass and age, while host-galaxy sSFR does not (beta = 0.042, p = 0.40) for the same clusters. The local model generalizes ~3x better under cross-validation (CV R^2 = 0.061 vs 0.022). The effect survives galaxy fixed effects (beta = 0.068, p = 0.001) and appears independently in each of the two galaxies large enough to fit alone. Including local Sigma_SFR reduces the mass coefficient by 26%.
AI.conclusion: The birth environment measurably shapes cluster structure, but only when measured on the scale on which clusters actually form; the earlier null result reflected an inappropriately large (galaxy-wide) measurement scale rather than an absence of environmental influence.

title: Beyond the dust: JWST reveals extinction and ice content in local (U)LIRGs
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A; 21 pages, 24 figures, 3 tables
summary: We investigate the spatially resolved extinction and ice column densities in four nearby interacting (U)LIRGs using JWST/NIRSpec integral field spectroscopy (R$\sim$2700; 0.97--5.14 $μ$m). This wide range encompasses numerous (>25) H recombination and H$_2$ ro-vibrational emission lines, as well as the prominent H$_2$O ($\sim$3.02 $μ$m) and CO$_2$ ($\sim$4.26 $μ$m) ice absorption features. We develop three methods to derive phase-specific extinction for ionized (A$_{\text K}^{\text HII}$) and hot molecular gas (A$_{\text K}^{\text H_2}$), and H$_2$O and CO$_2$ ice column densities (N$_{\text H_2O}$ and N$_{\text CO_2}$), exploiting H and H$_2$ emission lines and ice absorption features. Nuclear regions (0.2" radius) exhibit higher extinction and ice column densities than extended regions, with median A$_{\text K}^{\text HII}$ and A$_{\text K}^{\text H_2}$ of 1.25 and 0.75 in the nuclei, compared to 0.61 and 0.50 in the extended regions. The ionized gas is more extincted than the hot molecular gas, with A$_{\text K}^{\text HII}\approx1.5$ A$_{\text K}^{\text H_2}$, while H$_2$O ice column densities are comparable between phases. In some nuclei, continuum-derived N$_{\text H_2O}$ reaches $\sim10^{18.81}$ cm$^{-2}$, likely due to compact obscured components. These results suggest that ionized gas originates in more deeply embedded regions, whereas water ice envelopes both gas phases, with additional ice-rich material around the most obscured nuclei. The median N$_{\text CO_2}$/N$_{\text H_2O}$ abundance ratio is $\sim0.10$, a factor of 2--3 below typical Galactic values.

AI.tldr: Spatially resolved JWST/NIRSpec IFS of four nearby interacting (U)LIRGs reveals phase-specific dust extinction (ionized vs. hot molecular gas) and H2O/CO2 ice column densities, showing nuclear regions are more obscured and ice-rich than extended regions, with ionized gas more deeply embedded than hot molecular gas and sub-Galactic CO2/H2O ice ratios.
AI.motivation: Understanding dust extinction and ice chemistry in the dense, embedded regions of luminous infrared galaxies requires distinguishing between gas phases (ionized vs. hot molecular) and spatially resolving nuclear versus extended emission. Existing studies rarely provide phase-specific extinction together with ice column densities at matched spatial resolution, which is needed to determine where each gas phase originates and how ice mantles are distributed.
AI.method: JWST/NIRSpec integral field spectroscopy (R~2700, 0.97-5.14 micron) of four nearby interacting (U)LIRGs, covering >25 H recombination and H2 ro-vibrational emission lines plus H2O (~3.02 micron) and CO2 (~4.26 micron) ice absorption features. Three methods are developed to derive phase-specific extinction for ionized gas (A_K^HII) and hot molecular gas (A_K^H2), and to derive N_H2O and N_CO2 from emission lines and ice absorption, comparing nuclear (0.2" radius) and extended regions.
AI.result: Nuclei show higher extinction and ice column densities than extended regions: median A_K^HII and A_K^H2 of 1.25 and 0.75 in nuclei versus 0.61 and 0.50 in extended regions. Ionized gas is more extincted than hot molecular gas, with A_K^HII ~ 1.5 A_K^H2, while N_H2O is comparable between phases. Continuum-derived N_H2O reaches ~10^18.81 cm^-2 in some nuclei, likely tracing compact obscured components. The median N_CO2/N_H2O ratio is ~0.10, a factor 2-3 below typical Galactic values.
AI.conclusion: Ionized gas originates in more deeply embedded regions than hot molecular gas, whereas water ice envelopes both gas phases, with additional ice-rich material around the most obscured nuclei. The low CO2/H2O ice ratio (~0.10) indicates CO2-depleted or H2O-enriched ice chemistry relative to Galactic values in these (U)LIRG nuclei.

title: Beyond the Disc--Spheroid Dichotomy at $0.6 < z < 8.0$: Evidence for a Morphological Indeterminacy Regime from JWST
comment: 14 pages, 10 figures. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: Galaxy morphology is a fundamental tracer of galaxy assembly, but its characterization becomes increasingly uncertain in the early Universe. We investigate morphological classifications across different methodologies over the redshift range $0.6 < z < 8.0$, using JWST observations of 15,567 galaxies with 6,099 synthetic galaxies from IllustrisTNG. To quantify morphology without relying on visual labels or prescribed light profiles, we use an unsupervised-supervised hybrid machine-learning approach based on the non-parametric MEGG system, which combines the second moment of the light distribution, Entropy, Gini, and Gradient Pattern Analysis. We find that parametric and non-parametric classifications remain broadly consistent at $z < 2.5$, but diverge systematically at higher redshift. We identify this epoch as the Morphological Indeterminacy Regime (MIR), in which classical disc and spheroidal categories no longer provide a unique description of the galaxy population. The fraction of mixed-interpretation galaxies increases with redshift, reaching $F_{\rm MIR} \sim 0.55$ at $z > 2.5$. Cross-domain and projection-invariance tests show that the classifications are stable and insensitive to data set and viewing angle. In the interval $2.5 < z < 8.0$, MIR galaxies occupy an intermediate stellar-mass regime (median; $\log(M_\star/M_\odot) \sim 9.7$), between low-mass discs (median; $\log(M_\star/M_\odot) \sim 9.5$) and massive spheroids (median; $\log(M_\star/M_\odot) \sim 10.1$), while irregular systems have stellar-mass distributions similar to those of MIR galaxies. We interpret these results as evidence that morphological indeterminacy is a characteristic feature of galaxy assembly in the early Universe, reflecting a population of dynamically young systems that have not yet settled into the classical Hubble sequence.

AI.tldr: Using JWST (15,567 galaxies) plus IllustrisTNG synthetics (6,099), the authors show parametric and non-parametric morphology classifications agree at z<2.5 but diverge above it, defining a "Morphological Indeterminacy Regime" (F_MIR ~ 0.55 at z>2.5) populated by intermediate-mass, dynamically young systems.
AI.motivation: Galaxy morphology traces assembly, but characterizing it in the early Universe is increasingly uncertain; the paper tests whether classical morphological classifications remain meaningful at high redshift.
AI.method: Unsupervised-supervised hybrid machine-learning approach built on the non-parametric MEGG system (second moment of light distribution, Entropy, Gini, Gradient Pattern Analysis), applied to JWST observations of 15,567 galaxies and 6,099 IllustrisTNG synthetic galaxies over 0.6<z<8.0, with cross-domain and projection-invariance tests.
AI.result: Parametric and non-parametric classifications agree at z<2.5 and diverge systematically at higher z; mixed-interpretation fraction rises to F_MIR~0.55 at z>2.5. Classifications are stable and insensitive to dataset and viewing angle. In 2.5<z<8.0, MIR galaxies have median log(M*/Msun)~9.7, between low-mass discs (~9.5) and massive spheroids (~10.1), with irregulars showing similar mass distributions.
AI.conclusion: Morphological indeterminacy is a characteristic feature of early-Universe galaxy assembly, reflecting dynamically young systems that have not yet settled into the classical Hubble sequence.

title: Can Blue UV-Bright Galaxies Drive Reionization at Cosmic Dawn? An $M_{\rm UV}=-19.6$ Galaxy with $f_{\rm esc}\approx0.85$ at $z=9.244$
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ApJL. Comments welcome!
summary: We revisit EBG-1, a gravitationally lensed galaxy at $z = 9.244$, using newly obtained deep (14 hr) JWST/NIRSpec G235M ($R \sim 1000$) spectroscopy. EBG-1 is one of the bluest galaxies observed at $z > 9$. Along with its remarkably blue continuum of $β= -2.99 \pm 0.15$, we find very weak nebular emission from EBG-1. We obtain a $3σ$ upper limit of EW $< 8.4$ Angstrom for C III], a marginal H$β$ measurement (EW $= 256.2 \pm 122.2$ Angstrom), and a $5σ$ detection of [O III] $λ5007$ (EW $= 882.8 \pm 180.6$ Angstrom). These lines suggest an oxygen abundance of $12 + \log(\mathrm{O/H}) = 7.16 \pm 0.25$ ($\simeq 3\% Z_{\odot}$) and $\log(\mathrm{C/O}) < -0.88$ ($3σ$), placing EBG-1 on the C/O-metallicity sequence traced by lower-redshift galaxies. To constrain the escape fraction ($f_{\rm esc}$), we compare the observed UV slope and emission-line equivalent widths with synthetic spectra generated using BEAGLE. The models favor $f_{\rm esc} \gtrsim 0.75$, with $f_{\rm esc} \approx 0.85$ providing the best overall agreement with the observations. These results suggest that relatively UV-bright galaxies like EBG-1 can achieve the exceptionally high ionizing efficiencies supported by late reionization scenarios.

AI.tldr: Deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy of the ultrabright lensed galaxy EBG-1 at z=9.244 reveals an extremely blue UV continuum combined with very weak nebular emission lines, implying a very low oxygen abundance (~3% solar) and a high ionizing photon escape fraction of ~0.85, supporting scenarios in which UV-bright galaxies drive late reionization.
AI.motivation: Understanding which galaxies provided the ionizing photons that reionized the universe requires measuring escape fractions (f_esc) at z>9, yet such constraints are scarce. EBG-1, one of the bluest known galaxies at z>9, is an ideal laboratory because its blue continuum and weak emission lines are signatures expected from high ionizing efficiency. The authors aim to test whether relatively UV-bright galaxies can sustain the high f_esc required by late reionization models.
AI.method: The authors obtained deep (14 hr) JWST/NIRSpec G235M (R~1000) spectroscopy of the gravitationally lensed galaxy EBG-1 at z=9.244. They measured the UV continuum slope and the equivalent widths of C III], Hβ, and [O III] λ5007, deriving the oxygen abundance and C/O ratio. To constrain f_esc, they compared the observed UV slope and emission-line EWs with synthetic spectra generated with the BEAGLE spectral-fitting code.
AI.result: The continuum is extremely blue (β = -2.99 ± 0.15), while nebular emission is weak: a 3σ upper limit EW < 8.4 Å for C III], a marginal Hβ detection (EW = 256.2 ± 122.2 Å), and a 5σ [O III] λ5007 detection (EW = 882.8 ± 180.6 Å). These yield 12 + log(O/H) = 7.16 ± 0.25 (~3% Z_sun) and log(C/O) < -0.88 (3σ), placing EBG-1 on the C/O-metallicity sequence traced by lower-redshift galaxies. BEAGLE modeling favors f_esc ≳ 0.75, with f_esc ≈ 0.85 giving the best overall agreement.
AI.conclusion: Relatively UV-bright galaxies like EBG-1 can achieve the exceptionally high ionizing efficiencies (f_esc ≈ 0.85) demanded by late reionization scenarios. This supports the picture that such galaxies are viable major contributors to the reionizing photon budget at z>9.

title: Multiline Spectropolarimetric Evidence for Photospheric Reconnection in Ellerman Bombs from DKIST
comment: accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: Ellerman bombs (EBs) are compact, transient brightenings observed in the wings of Balmer lines and are believed to result from magnetic reconnection in the lower solar atmosphere. However, their signatures have rarely been observed simultaneously in multiple spectral lines sensitive to the lower atmosphere. We present novel high-resolution multiline spectropolarimetric observations of EBs obtained with the Visible Spectro-Polarimeter (ViSP) on the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST). Simultaneous observations reveal remarkable H$β$ wing enhancements extending up to $\sim$4~Å from the line core and intensity enhancements in the \ion{Na}{1}~D1 and \ion{Fe}{1}~6302 lines. Using multiline non-LTE inversion of the \ion{Na}{1} and \ion{Fe}{1} lines, we infer localized photospheric heating of up to $ΔT\sim$800~K, accompanied by weak upflows and downflows at EB locations. Comparing with synthetic observables from Bifrost radiative-MHD simulations, we find that synthetic spectra reproduce the observed H$β$ and \ion{Na}{1}~D wing enhancements and yield atmospheric stratification broadly consistent with those inferred from the non-LTE inversion. This study provides strong evidence that EBs are driven by photospheric magnetic reconnection below the temperature-minimum region, and places new constraints on the realistic EB models and small-scale energy release in the lower solar atmosphere.

AI.tldr: Novel DKIST/ViSP multiline spectropolarimetry of Ellerman bombs reveals Hβ wing enhancements up to ~4 Å and Na I D1/Fe I 6302 brightenings; non-LTE inversion yields localized photospheric heating up to ΔT~800 K with weak up/downflows, and Bifrost MHD synthetics reproduce the observations, supporting photospheric reconnection below the temperature minimum.
AI.motivation: Ellerman bombs are compact transient brightenings in Balmer wings thought to arise from magnetic reconnection in the lower solar atmosphere, but their signatures have rarely been observed simultaneously across multiple spectral lines sensitive to that region, leaving their formation height and energetics poorly constrained.
AI.method: High-resolution simultaneous spectropolarimetric observations with DKIST/ViSP covering Hβ, Na I D1 and Fe I 6302; multiline non-LTE inversion of Na I and Fe I to derive atmospheric stratification; comparison with synthetic observables from Bifrost radiative-MHD simulations.
AI.result: Hβ wing enhancements extending to ~4 Å from line core plus intensity enhancements in Na I D1 and Fe I 6302; non-LTE inversion infers localized photospheric heating up to ΔT~800 K with weak upflows and downflows at EB locations; Bifrost synthetics reproduce the Hβ and Na I D wing enhancements and give stratification broadly consistent with the inversion.
AI.conclusion: The simultaneous multiline evidence indicates EBs are driven by photospheric magnetic reconnection occurring below the temperature-minimum region, providing new constraints on realistic EB models and small-scale energy release in the lower solar atmosphere.

title: Spiraling into the `snail' cluster MCXC J0157.4-0550
comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: We present a deep Chandra (130 ks) study of a striking, tidally induced cold front in a subcluster merging with the galaxy cluster MCXC J0157.4-0550. The subcluster, nicknamed the `snail' (J0157), displays an extensive spiral structure that extends to $\sim 260$ kpc --- one of the largest spiral cold fronts identified to date. Surface brightness and spectral analysis across four sectors reveal a consistent density jump of a factor of $\sim 3$ across the front, together with significant temperature discontinuities, and thermodynamic mapping further delineates the coherent, low-entropy structure of the stripped gas. Unlike classical sloshing cold fronts, the spiral in J0157 arises not from oscillation of a displaced cool core, but from subcluster gas that has been ram pressure stripped and tidally wound into a spiral by orbital rotation. Applying Gaussian Gradient Magnitude filtering and azimuthal surface-brightness analysis, we identify quasi-periodic corrugations along the front consistent with candidate Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) instabilities, with a characteristic scale of $\sim 90$ kpc. The presence of these KH rolls constrains the effective ICM viscosity to $\lesssim 0.59$ times the Spitzer value and the magnetic field strength at the interface to $\lesssim 5.9\ μ$G. These results establish J0157 as a useful laboratory for probing macro-scale merger-induced gas dynamics and micro-scale plasma transport processes in the intracluster medium.

AI.tldr: A 130 ks Chandra study of a giant (~260 kpc) tidally wound "snail" cold front in subcluster J0157 reveals a ram-pressure-stripped, tidally rolled spiral gas structure whose ~90 kpc corrugations are candidate Kelvin-Helmholtz rolls, constraining ICM viscosity to ≲0.59 Spitzer and interface magnetic field to ≲5.9 μG.
AI.motivation: Classical sloshing cold fronts arise from oscillation of a displaced cool core, but subcluster mergers can instead produce tidally induced, ram-pressure-stripped spiral cold fronts. Such systems offer a laboratory for probing merger-driven gas dynamics and micro-scale plasma transport (viscosity, magnetic fields) in the intracluster medium; the authors aim to characterize one of the largest known spiral cold fronts, J0157.
AI.method: Deep Chandra observation (130 ks) of the subcluster merging with MCXC J0157.4-0550. Surface brightness and spectral analysis across four sectors to measure density jumps and temperature discontinuities; thermodynamic mapping of entropy structure; Gaussian Gradient Magnitude filtering plus azimuthal surface-brightness analysis to detect quasi-periodic corrugations interpreted as Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities.
AI.result: The spiral structure extends to ~260 kpc, one of the largest spiral cold fronts known. Four sectors show a consistent density jump of ~3 across the front, along with significant temperature discontinuities and a coherent low-entropy stripped-gas structure. Quasi-periodic corrugations with characteristic scale ~90 kpc are identified along the front, consistent with candidate KH instabilities. These imply an effective ICM viscosity ≲0.59 times Spitzer and interface magnetic field ≲5.9 μG.
AI.conclusion: Unlike classical sloshing cold fronts, the J0157 spiral originates from ram-pressure-stripped subcluster gas tidally wound by orbital rotation. The KH-roll constraints establish J0157 as a valuable laboratory for studying macro-scale merger-induced gas dynamics and micro-scale plasma transport in the ICM.

title: A Two-Population von Mises--Fisher Distribution of the Magnetic Field Direction in the Young Solar Wind
comment: submitted to ApJL
summary: The one-point distribution of the magnetic field direction in the young solar wind is found to be a superposition of two populations rather than a single exponential. Using Parker Solar Probe (PSP) Encounter 1 magnetometer data, we show that the distribution of the pitch-angle cosine mu(t) = bhat(t) . bhat_0 is well described by a two-component von Mises-Fisher (vMF) mixture: a broad, weakly confined component of concentration kappa_1 ~ 3.6 that accounts for the large-amplitude rotations and switchback tail, and a field-aligned component that reduces, in the small-angle limit, to a Gaussian in the polar angle theta of width sigma ~ 15 degrees (concentration kappa_2 ~ 14). The concentration of the field-aligned component is not a free parameter: it is set by the level of the transverse Alfvenic fluctuation through kappa_2 = 2<|B|^2>/<delta B_perp^2> = 2/<1-mu^2> ~ 16.2, in agreement with the fitted value to within ~12%. The transverse fluctuations are weakly anisotropic (<delta B_1^2>/<delta B_2^2> ~ 1.1), so the core is a weakly anisotropic Bingham distribution rather than a pure vMF. The broad component is exponential in mu, not in theta, confirming that switchbacks saturate toward mu = -1 rather than decaying away, consistent with the drift-diffusion framework of Bian et al. (2024, ApJ, 960, L15). This physics-based two-population framework connects macroscopic fluid parameters directly to those describing the directional statistics, offering a powerful diagnostic for probing the structural evolution of MHD turbulence and switchbacks in the inner heliosphere.

AI.tldr: The one-point distribution of magnetic field direction in the young solar wind is a two-component von Mises-Fisher (vMF) mixture rather than a single exponential: a broad, weakly confined component (kappa_1 ~ 3.6) capturing large-amplitude rotations and switchbacks, plus a field-aligned component whose concentration kappa_2 is set by the transverse Alfvenic fluctuation level (kappa_2 = 2<|B|^2>/<delta B_perp^2> ~ 16.2), matching the fitted value within ~12%.
AI.motivation: Prior descriptions treated the one-point distribution of magnetic field direction in the young solar wind as a single exponential. The authors aim to show that this distribution is in fact a superposition of two physically distinct populations, and to connect the directional statistics directly to macroscopic fluid (turbulence) parameters.
AI.method: Using Parker Solar Probe Encounter 1 magnetometer data, the authors fit the pitch-angle cosine distribution mu(t) = bhat(t)·bhat_0 with a two-component vMF mixture. They relate the field-aligned component's concentration to the transverse Alfvenic fluctuation level via kappa_2 = 2<|B|^2>/<delta B_perp^2> = 2/<1-mu^2>, and assess transverse anisotropy to model the core as a weakly anisotropic Bingham distribution.
AI.result: A broad, weakly confined component (kappa_1 ~ 3.6) accounts for large-amplitude rotations and the switchback tail; a field-aligned component reduces, in the small-angle limit, to a Gaussian in polar angle theta with sigma ~ 15 degrees (kappa_2 ~ 14). The predicted kappa_2 ~ 16.2 agrees with the fitted value to within ~12%. Transverse fluctuations are weakly anisotropic (<delta B_1^2>/<delta B_2^2> ~ 1.1). The broad component is exponential in mu (not theta), confirming switchbacks saturate toward mu = -1 rather than decaying away, consistent with the drift-diffusion framework of Bian et al. (2024).
AI.conclusion: The directional statistics of the young solar wind magnetic field are well described by a physics-based two-population framework that links macroscopic fluid parameters directly to those governing directional statistics, providing a powerful diagnostic for probing structural evolution of MHD turbulence and switchbacks in the inner heliosphere.

title: Statistical Strong Lensing V. Inference with Microlensed Quasars
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Microlensing of strongly lensed quasars provides direct information on the stellar component of lens galaxies, and can help break the degeneracy between the stellar initial mass function (IMF) and the dark matter. However, a statistical framework to forward model microlensing data while accounting for strong lensing selection effects is still missing. We incorporated microlensing effects into the hierarchical model of Paper III, and investigated to what extent flux measurements of strongly lensed quasars can break the degeneracy between the stellar IMF and the dark matter distribution. We tested the method on a mock sample of 219 doubly imaged quasars, lensed by circularly symmetric lenses. When microlensing effects are modelled, the inference using image fluxes recovers the input foreground population parameters and provides tighter constraints than the inference without flux constraints. The improvement is clearest in the $μ_α-μ_5$ plane, where $μ_α$ describes the mean stellar population synthesis mismatch parameter $\logα_{\rm SPS}$ and $μ_5$ describes the mean projected dark matter mass within $5\,{\rm kpc}$. The 68% credible interval on $μ_α$ shrinks from 0.16 dex to 0.09 dex, with the degeneracy between $μ_α$ and $μ_5$ significantly reduced. By contrast, fitting the image fluxes without accounting for microlensing leads to large biases on the inferred parameters. This work is a first step towards an accurate modelling of microlensing data. Application to real lens samples will require dropping the circular symmetry assumption and adopting more realistic models for the microlensing magnification.

AI.tldr: Incorporating microlensing into a hierarchical forward model of strongly lensed quasars breaks the IMF–dark matter degeneracy, shrinking the 68% credible interval on the mean SPS mismatch parameter from 0.16 to 0.09 dex.
AI.motivation: Microlensing of strongly lensed quasars directly probes the stellar component of lens galaxies and can break the degeneracy between the stellar IMF and dark matter, but no statistical framework existed to forward model microlensing data while accounting for strong lensing selection effects.
AI.method: The authors extend the hierarchical model of Paper III to include microlensing effects, then test it on a mock sample of 219 doubly imaged quasars lensed by circularly symmetric lenses, comparing inference with and without modeling microlensing.
AI.result: When microlensing is modeled, image-flux inference recovers the input foreground population parameters with tighter constraints; the 68% credible interval on μ_α shrinks from 0.16 dex to 0.09 dex and the μ_α–μ_5 degeneracy is significantly reduced. Ignoring microlensing in the fit produces large parameter biases.
AI.conclusion: This is a first step toward accurate microlensing modeling; application to real lens samples requires dropping circular symmetry and adopting more realistic microlensing magnification models.

title: Mass-loss Rates of 74 Bow Shock OB Stars: No Evidence for Bi-stability Behavior
comment: 36 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables
summary: Accurate measurements of wind-driven mass-loss rates are essential for understanding the evolution and fate of massive stars. Established techniques for measuring $\dot{M}$ suffer from large dispersions and become insensitive in the regime of weak-winded late-O to early B stars. We employ a promising new technique to measure stellar mass loss for \numstars~early type stars that produce infrared stellar bow shock nebulae. We use updated stellar parameters, improved parallactic distances and proper motions, and modern dust models to characterize the bow shock nebulae and obtain new measurements of mass-loss rates. $\mdot$ ranges from $2\times10^{-9}~\moperyear$ for weak-winded late-O and early B stars at $\log\left(\lstar/L_\odot\right)\approx4.5$ to $4\times10^{-6}~\moperyear$ for the most luminous stars in our sample at $\log\left(\lstar/L_\odot\right)\approx6.3$. Stellar space velocities relative to their local standard of rest are insufficient to accurately reflect the relative star-ISM velocities for the majority of our sample, which have speeds much less than canonical runaway thresholds, suggesting the pervasive influence of bulk interstellar flows in forming bow shock nebulae. Adopting a minimum relative velocity of $20~\kms$ is physically motivated and yields mass-loss rates in excellent agreement with the latest theoretical prescriptions while requiring no adjustable parameters. We find no enhancements in $\mdot$ for stars cooler than 25~kK, in agreement with modern mass-loss recipes that do not include bi-stability effects.

AI.tldr: Using infrared bow shock nebulae around early-type stars, the authors measure wind mass-loss rates spanning 2×10⁻⁹ to 4×10⁻⁶ M☉/yr, finding agreement with modern theoretical prescriptions when a minimum star–ISM relative velocity of 20 km/s is adopted, and no mass-loss enhancement below 25 kK.
AI.motivation: Accurate wind-driven mass-loss rates are critical for understanding massive star evolution, but established measurement techniques show large dispersion and lose sensitivity for weak-winded late-O to early-B stars. A new, independent diagnostic is therefore needed.
AI.method: The authors apply a bow-shock-based technique to a sample of early-type stars that produce infrared stellar bow shock nebulae, using updated stellar parameters, improved parallactic distances and proper motions, and modern dust models to characterize the nebulae and derive mass-loss rates.
AI.result: Mass-loss rates range from 2×10⁻⁹ M☉/yr for weak-winded late-O/early-B stars at log(L/L☉)≈4.5 up to 4×10⁻⁶ M☉/yr for the most luminous stars at log(L/L☉)≈6.3. Space velocities relative to the local standard of rest are inadequate proxies for star–ISM relative velocities for most of the sample, implying bulk interstellar flows shape the bow shocks. Adopting a minimum relative velocity of 20 km/s yields rates in excellent agreement with the latest theoretical prescriptions without adjustable parameters. No mass-loss enhancement is found for stars cooler than 25 kK.
AI.conclusion: Bow shock nebulae provide a viable, parameter-free probe of stellar mass loss that resolves weaknesses of conventional diagnostics. The results support modern mass-loss recipes that omit bi-stability effects and highlight the role of bulk interstellar flows in bow shock formation.

title: Newly Identified Planetary Nebula Candidates in M31 using Deep-Learning Search of Hubble Space Telescope Images
comment: 28 pages, 13 figures, 5 tables, Submitted to PASP
summary: The Hubble Space Telescope has imaged approximately a quarter of a billion stars in M31's disc, yet only slightly over a thousand planetary nebulae (PNe) are known, mostly from ground-based surveys. We show that deep learning can find them in broad-band images alone. In what is the first such search, we scan the Panchromatic Hubble Andromeda Treasury (PHAT) and the Panchromatic Hubble Andromeda Southern Treasury (PHAST) mosaics, nearly one square degree of the disk, where a PN is a faint blue point among crowded stars. Because the existing catalogs are incomplete, we train four Faster R-CNN detectors with partial supervision, so that uncataloged PNe are not taught as background, and combine their rankings into one candidate list, an ensemble. On spatially separate test fields, this list places 73% of the known PNe in its top 200, 4 to 6 times the purity of classical color-magnitude selection. Newer detection transformers and segmentation networks trained on the same data do not surpass our detectors. The ranking also follows classifications that the detectors never saw: emission-line objects that the literature calls PNe enter the list at 47%, against 0.6% for those called H II regions, which makes them candidates for reclassification. Among the top 400 candidates, 175 appear in no published catalog, 12 of them flagged as cosmic-ray residuals. One of them, a point source with [O III] emission in nine independent exposures, meets the PN criteria of the three major PN studies of M31, so by those criteria it is a PN. Most of the others lack strong [O III], as expected if narrow-band surveys have found the bright PNe, although some may be PNe with weak [O III]. These results support the near completeness of ground-based surveys for bright PNe and extend it from the PHAT area to PHAST. Finally, we identify evaluation pitfalls for detectors of rare objects and recommend simple remedies.

AI.tldr: Deep learning with partially supervised Faster R-CNN detectors finds planetary nebulae in M31 from broad-band Hubble images alone, achieving 73% recall of known PNe within the top 200 ranked candidates (4–6× the purity of color-magnitude selection) and revealing 175 uncataloged candidates.
AI.motivation: Approximately 250 million stars have been imaged in M31's disc, yet only ~1,000 planetary nebulae are known, mostly from ground-based narrow-band surveys, leaving the catalogs incomplete. The authors aim to demonstrate that PNe—faint blue point sources in crowded stellar fields—can be detected in broad-band images alone, and to extend coverage from the PHAT region to the larger PHAST area.
AI.method: The authors scan the PHAT and PHAST mosaics (~1 sq. deg) and train four Faster R-CNN detectors under partial supervision, so uncataloged PNe are not learned as background, then ensemble their rankings into a single candidate list. They benchmark against detection transformers and segmentation networks trained on the same data, validate on spatially separate test fields, and assess rankings against literature classifications (PNe vs. H II regions) never seen in training. They also identify evaluation pitfalls for rare-object detectors.
AI.result: On held-out test fields, the ensemble places 73% of known PNe in its top 200, 4–6× the purity of classical color-magnitude selection; newer DETR and segmentation models do not surpass the detectors. Emission-line objects literature-labeled as PNe enter the list at 47% vs. 0.6% for H II regions. Among the top 400 candidates, 175 appear in no published catalog (12 flagged as cosmic-ray residuals); one—a point source with [O III] emission in nine independent exposures—meets the PN criteria of three major M31 studies.
AI.conclusion: The results support near-completeness of ground-based surveys for bright PNe and extend this completeness from the PHAT to the PHAST area, while most new candidates lacking strong [O III] are consistent with narrow-band surveys already capturing bright PNe (some may be weak-[O III] PNe). The work also surfaces evaluation pitfalls for detectors of rare objects and offers simple remedies.

title: Intermittent turbulence as the driver of stochastic heating in the near-Sun solar wind
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures
summary: Understanding the mechanism by which the energy is dissipated at small scales to heat the outer corona and expanding solar wind, is a primary goal of the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission, and an outstanding question in heliophysics. Recent observational case studies have suggested that the dominant dissipation mechanism(s), stochastic heating (SH) or resonant heating (RH), may be modulated by the Alfvén `surface' ($M_A = 1$), while theoretical and simulation works predict that the mechanism should be modulated by the level of turbulence imbalance. We measure the local energy transfer (LET) rate from $9.8$ to $55$ solar radii from PSP observations, showing that the LET rate peaks at $M_A \sim 0.4 - 0.9$. We connect enhanced LET rates to signatures of intermittency, highlighting the key role that intermittent fluctuations play in heating the near-Sun solar wind. We compare the LET rate with estimates of the SH rate, finding that below $\sim 15$ solar radii the SH heating rate matches the LET rate provided intermittency is accounted for, regardless of $M_A$, while farther from the Sun, SH is unable to account for the observed LET rate. In contrast to predictions by recent theoretical works, this implies that `imbalanced' intermittent stochastic heating may be a viable mechanism to heat highly imbalanced, low-$β$ collisionless plasmas, and is likely an important mechanism of dissipation in the outer solar corona and near-Sun solar wind.

AI.tldr: Local energy transfer (LET) rates measured by Parker Solar Probe peak at M_A ~ 0.4–0.9 and correlate with intermittency; stochastic heating can account for LET within ~15 solar radii when intermittency is included, regardless of M_A, but not farther out.
AI.motivation: The dissipation mechanism converting small-scale energy into heat for the outer corona and solar wind is a central Parker Solar Probe question. Observed case studies suggest modulation by the Alfvén surface (M_A = 1), while theory/simulations predict modulation by turbulence imbalance—these competing predictions need observational testing.
AI.method: Measure the local energy transfer (LET) rate from 9.8 to 55 solar radii using PSP observations; relate enhanced LET to intermittency signatures; compare LET with estimates of the stochastic heating (SH) rate, accounting for intermittency and M_A.
AI.result: LET rate peaks at M_A ~ 0.4–0.9; enhanced LET is linked to intermittency. Below ~15 solar radii, the SH rate matches LET once intermittency is included, independent of M_A; beyond this, SH cannot explain the observed LET rate.
AI.conclusion: Contrary to recent theoretical predictions, imbalanced intermittent stochastic heating appears viable for heating highly imbalanced, low-β collisionless plasmas, and is likely an important dissipation mechanism in the outer corona and near-Sun solar wind.

title: Forecasting the Resolvability of Stellar Velocity Dispersions in Ultra-faint Dwarf Galaxies
comment: 14 pages + 3 appendix, 14 figures, 1 table. To be submitted to Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs)---the smallest and most dark-matter dominated galactic systems---push the boundaries of our understanding of galaxy formation in the cold dark matter paradigm. As current and near-future imaging surveys continue to expand the known population of extremely faint systems, spectroscopic resources have become a major limitation in our ability to understand the physical nature of these systems. We present projections for the capability of Keck/DEIMOS, Magellan/IMACS, and future spectroscopic instruments (e.g., Magellan/Via and GMT/GMACS) to kinematically distinguish dark-matter-dominated UFDs from dark-matter-free star clusters in the ultra-faint regime. We simulate ensembles of mock observations of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies and apply a formal statistical framework, calibrated to observations, to systematically characterize the ability to resolve velocity dispersions as a function of satellite properties. Our projections suggest that current instruments will struggle to resolve many of systems that will be discovered by the Rubin Observatory. Near future instruments will be capable of resolving a majority of these systems, though they will fail for the faintest and most distant systems. Ultimately, we will require even more advanced instruments, with enhanced stability and velocity precision, to classify the full population of ultra-faint Milky Way satellites.

AI.tldr: Mock-observation forecasts show that current spectrographs (Keck/DEIMOS, Magellan/IMACS) will fail to resolve velocity dispersions for many ultra-faint dwarf galaxies found by Rubin, near-future instruments (Magellan/Via, GMT/GMACS) will succeed for most, and only advanced, highly stable high-precision spectrographs can classify the full population.
AI.motivation: Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies are the smallest, most dark-matter-dominated galactic systems and probe galaxy formation in the cold dark matter paradigm. Imaging surveys are rapidly expanding the known population of extremely faint systems, but spectroscopic follow-up capacity is now the limiting factor for establishing their physical nature—specifically, distinguishing dark-matter-dominated UFDs from dark-matter-free star clusters.
AI.method: The authors generate ensembles of mock spectroscopic observations of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies and apply a formal statistical framework, calibrated to real observations, to systematically characterize the ability to resolve velocity dispersions as a function of satellite properties. They project the performance of Keck/DEIMOS, Magellan/IMACS, and future instruments (Magellan/Via, GMT/GMACS).
AI.result: Current instruments struggle to resolve velocity dispersions for many systems that Rubin Observatory will discover. Near-future instruments can resolve the majority of these systems but fail for the faintest and most distant ones. Classifying the full population of ultra-faint Milky Way satellites requires even more advanced instruments with enhanced stability and velocity precision.
AI.conclusion: Spectroscopic capability, not imaging, is the key bottleneck in characterizing the ultra-faint satellite population; a staged progression of instrumentation is needed, culminating in next-generation high-stability, high-velocity-precision spectrographs to fully distinguish UFDs from star clusters.

title: Magnetic-field constraints for four magnetic cataclysmic variables from simultaneous continuum and cyclotron modeling
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 22 pages, 11 figures
summary: their fields are rarely measured because cyclotron humps must be separated from uncertain continua and assigned to discrete harmonics. We applied a simultaneous continuum-cyclotron analysis to four DESI/LAMOST magnetic-CV candidates. We fit a white dwarf atmospheric model, a hot-spot blackbody, and an isothermal constant-$Λ$ cyclotron component in one inverse-variance weighted model. J0022+1340 has two indistinguishable branches at $B \simeq 64.4$ and 77.7 MG; J0749+3654 has competitive solutions near 29.3 and 96.4 MG; and J0035+4333 yields an indicative broad minimum at $B = 51.1\pm1.4$ MG. AI.motivation: Magnetic field strengths in magnetic cataclysmic variables (CVs) are rarely measured because cyclotron humps must be disentangled from uncertain continua and assigned to discrete harmonics, creating degeneracies in the field determination.

title: The Impact of an AGN on PAH Spectral Features in Galaxy Evolution Simulations: Continuum Dilution and Excitation of PAHs
comment: Submitted to ApJ. 13 pages, 8 figures
summary: Galaxies hosting an active galactic nucleus (AGN) show diminished power and non-standard spectral feature ratios from polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) compared with normal star-forming galaxies. Proposed mechanisms for this difference include a combination of AGN-driven PAH grain processing, differential heating from the surrounding radiation field, and continuum dilution. These potentially competing factors are difficult to disentangle observationally. In this paper, we investigate the impact of the AGN radiation field on the excitation properties and potential dilution of the mid-IR emission features via constrained numerical experiments of idealized galaxies in simulations that include a self-consistent model for the evolution of dust. We find that, for the integrated spectrum of our simulated Milky Way analog and independent of grain-processing physics, the apparent PAH emission is progressively diminished as AGN luminosity is increased. For spectra within the central half kiloparsec, PAH features are entirely obfuscated when an AGN of any sampled luminosity is present. We additionally find that the UV radiation from an AGN is capable of impacting PAH band ratios, though note that we do not yet include a model for potential photodestruction of PAHs. Our model suggests that the inferred lack of PAHs via featureless mid-IR spectra from galaxies hosting AGN may simply owe to the direct continuum from the AGN overpowering mid-IR features from PAHs in the ISM of the host galaxy. Future work will investigate the relative role of AGN continuum dilution and PAH heating vs photodestruction/ionization of PAHs.

AI.tldr: Idealized simulated galaxies show that the apparent deficit of PAH emission in AGN hosts can arise simply from AGN continuum dilution overwhelming mid-IR PAH features, independent of grain-processing physics.
AI.motivation: AGN hosts exhibit reduced PAH power and anomalous PAH band ratios relative to normal star-forming galaxies, but the competing explanations (AGN-driven grain processing, differential heating by the surrounding radiation field, and continuum dilution) are hard to disentangle observationally. The paper aims to isolate the role of the AGN radiation field.
AI.method: Constrained numerical experiments on idealized galaxies in simulations that include a self-consistent dust evolution model, varying AGN luminosity and examining integrated versus central-half-kiloparsec spectra, while excluding explicit PAH photodestruction.
AI.result: For the integrated spectrum of a simulated Milky Way analog, apparent PAH emission diminishes progressively with increasing AGN luminosity regardless of grain-processing physics. Within the central 0.5 kpc, PAH features are entirely obfuscated for any sampled AGN luminosity. AGN UV radiation can also alter PAH band ratios, although photodestruction is not yet modeled.
AI.conclusion: The inferred lack of PAHs from featureless mid-IR spectra of AGN hosts may simply result from the AGN's direct continuum overpowering PAH features in the host ISM. Future work will separate the relative contributions of continuum dilution, PAH heating, and photodestruction/ionization.

title: Granulation in Color: The Chromatic Stellar Flicker of LTT-9779 and WASP-121
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to A&A
summary:
Granulation is a persistent feature of stars with outer convective layers and is the photospheric signature of near-surface convective energy transport. In disk-integrated observations, it produces stochastic brightness variations that contribute substantially to stellar variability on timescales of minutes to hours. High-precision, observations with JWST provide an opportunity to study the chromatic signatures of stellar granulation.
  This work aims to measure the amplitude and characteristic timescale of granulation-induced variability for solar-type stars and to investigate whether the granulation signal shows significant chromatic variation in the near-infrared.
  We accessed publicly available JWST/NIRISS SOSS time-series observations of LTT-9779 (G7V) and WASP-121 (F6V) and de-trended the light curves by fitting the transits, eclipses, and planetary phase curves. We computed power spectra from the de-trended light curves and fit them with a Harvey granulation profile. We first analyzed the broadband light curves to measure and fix the granulation timescale and then repeated the power-spectrum analysis in individual wavelength channels to measure the chromatic dependence of the granulation amplitude.
  For LTT-9779, we measure a broadband granulation amplitude of σ$=53.8^{+4.1}_{-4.0}$ppm at a timescale of τ$=4.8^{+1.5}_{-1.3}$min. For WASP-121, we measure σ$=59.3\pm4.3$ppm and τ$=6.3^{+2.1}_{-1.8}$min. We also measure peak oscillation frequencies of ν$=3382^{+166}_{-191}μ$Hz and $1649^{+55}_{-69}μ$Hz in the bandpass-integrated power spectra of LTT-9779 and WASP-121, respectively. In the spectroscopic fits, we find $σ$ decreases with wavelength. Our results demonstrate a new observational window on short-timescale stellar variability and provides a way to characterize chromatic stellar noise in transit light curves.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRISS SOSS light curves of LTT-9779 (G7V) and WASP-121 (F6V) show granulation amplitudes of ~54-59 ppm at ~5-6 min timescales, with amplitude decreasing toward longer wavelengths in the near-infrared.
AI.motivation: Granulation is a pervasive photospheric signature of near-surface convection in cool stars, producing stochastic brightness variations on minute-to-hour timescales that contribute significantly to disk-integrated stellar variability. JWST's high precision offers a new opportunity to characterize the chromatic behavior of this granulation noise, which is relevant for disentangling stellar signals from transit/eclipse measurements.
AI.method: Publicly available JWST/NIRISS SOSS time-series observations of LTT-9779 and WASP-121 were de-trended by fitting transits, eclipses, and planetary phase curves. Power spectra of the de-trended light curves were computed and fit with a Harvey granulation profile. Broadband light curves were first used to measure and fix the granulation timescale; the power-spectrum analysis was then repeated in individual wavelength channels to measure the chromatic dependence of the granulation amplitude.
AI.result: LTT-9779: broadband granulation amplitude σ = 53.8 (+4.1/-4.0) ppm, timescale τ = 4.8 (+1.5/-1.3) min. WASP-121: σ = 59.3 ± 4.3 ppm, τ = 6.3 (+2.1/-1.8) min. Peak oscillation frequencies of ν = 3382 (+166/-191) µHz and 1649 (+55/-69) µHz were detected for LTT-9779 and WASP-121, respectively. Spectroscopic fits show σ decreasing with wavelength.
AI.conclusion: JWST NIR spectroscopy opens a new observational window on short-timescale stellar variability and provides a means to characterize chromatic stellar noise in transit light curves.

title: The Star Formation Histories of Different Components of M31's Halo from Photometric Estimates of Fe and $α$ Abundances
comment: 19 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: We present the chemical-abundance distributions and star-formation histories of the M31 halo components using photometric Fe and $α$ abundance estimates derived from the PAndAS broad-band $g$ and $i$ filters and the Subaru/HSC $NB515$ narrow-band filter. We selected about 76,400 candidate M31 giant stars and constructed a synthetic photometric training dataset based on model isochrones. We estimated elemental abundances and errors using random forest regression models. We identify various halo components, including about 32,500 stars in the ``smooth" halo (where ``smooth" refers to the complete sample with all the known substructures removed), and infer their star-formation histories from comparisons of their abundance distributions. From the radial abundance gradients, we find that [Fe/H] decreases while [$α$/Fe] increases toward the outer halo. Including substructures further enhances the radial abundance contrast, suggesting that the smooth halo stars are accreted at relatively early times, before the progenitor galaxies produce large numbers of Type Ia supernovae. Both M31 and the Milky Way show similar radial gradient trends, but M31 exhibits higher [Fe/H] and lower [$α$/Fe] values overall, suggesting that the smooth halo of M31 may possess a larger fraction of relatively younger stars associated with more recent merger events. Future photometric observations with additional narrow-band filters and larger spectroscopic samples are expected to provide a better understanding of the formation and evolution history of M31.

AI.tldr: Using PAndAS g,i plus Subaru/HSC NB515 photometry and random-forest regression, the authors derive Fe and alpha abundances for ~76,400 M31 giant stars to map halo components and their star-formation histories.
AI.motivation: The formation and assembly history of the M31 halo, particularly the accreted "smooth" component versus substructures, is poorly constrained; spatially resolved chemical abundances can disentangle accretion epochs.
AI.method: Photometric Fe and alpha abundance estimates from broad-band g, i and NB515 narrow-band filters; a synthetic training set built from model isochrones; random-forest regression to estimate abundances and uncertainties; separation of smooth halo (~32,500 stars) from substructures; analysis of radial abundance gradients and comparison with the Milky Way.
AI.result: [Fe/H] decreases and [alpha/Fe] increases toward the outer halo; substructures enhance the radial contrast. M31 shows the same gradient trends as the Milky Way but higher [Fe/H] and lower [alpha/Fe] overall.
AI.conclusion: Smooth-halo stars were accreted relatively early, before progenitor galaxies produced substantial Type Ia supernovae; M31's smooth halo may host a larger fraction of younger stars from more recent mergers. Additional narrow-band photometry and larger spectroscopic samples are needed.

title: Gravitational filtering, magnetic-field inhomogeneity and Coulomb collisions in a kinetic model of a plasma atmosphere with stochastic heating at its base
comment: 24 pages, 2 figures
summary: We investigate the effects of stochastic heating, magnetic inhomogeneity, and Coulomb collisions in coronal loops using a reduced kinetic model. Coulomb collisions thermalize suprathermal populations generated by intermittent heating and populate velocity-space regions inaccessible from the lower boundary in the collisionless limit. We consider two regimes: when heating varies faster than the electron crossing time, the plasma develops a multitemperature nonthermal distribution; when it varies more slowly than the proton crossing time, individual heated loops approach an isothermal state. In the collisionless limit, conservation of the magnetic moment restricts the accessible velocity space, producing a strong temperature anisotropy, with parallel temperature exceeding perpendicular temperature, and additional density depletion. We find that Coulomb pitch-angle scattering efficiently suppresses these effects under typical coronal conditions. In the short-time-scale regime, density and temperature profiles approach those obtained with a constant magnetic field, while gravitational and collisional filtering sustain the temperature inversion. In the strongly collisional long-time-scale regime, magnetic-field-induced anisotropy is nearly eliminated, and individual loops remain approximately isotropic and isothermal. An increasing temperature profile then emerges only after averaging over unresolved flux tubes with different temperatures. Thus, Coulomb collisions largely suppress the macroscopic kinetic signatures of magnetic-field inhomogeneity in the transition region and low corona.

AI.tldr: Using a reduced kinetic model, the authors show that Coulomb pitch-angle scattering largely erases the kinetic signatures (temperature anisotropy and density depletion) produced by magnetic moment conservation and stochastic heating in coronal loops, so that macroscopic profiles are governed mainly by collisionality regime and flux-tube averaging.
AI.motivation: Coronal loops are heated intermittently and threaded by inhomogeneous magnetic fields, yet it is unclear how stochastic heating, magnetic-field inhomogeneity, and Coulomb collisions jointly shape the electron velocity distribution and the resulting density and temperature profiles; in particular, whether collisionless magnetic-moment conservation leaves observable kinetic signatures in the transition region and low corona.
AI.method: A reduced kinetic model of coronal loops incorporating stochastic (intermittent) heating, magnetic-field inhomogeneity, and Coulomb collisions (pitch-angle scattering and thermalization of suprathermal populations). Two heating regimes are compared: heating varying faster than the electron crossing time (multitemperature, nonthermal distributions) and slower than the proton crossing time (near-isothermal loops). Collisionless-limit behaviour is contrasted with strongly collisional behaviour, and the role of gravitational and collisional filtering and averaging over unresolved flux tubes is examined.
AI.result: In the collisionless limit, magnetic-moment conservation restricts accessible velocity space, yielding strong temperature anisotropy with T_parallel > T_perp and additional density depletion. Coulomb pitch-angle scattering efficiently suppresses these effects under typical coronal conditions. In the short-time-scale regime, density and temperature profiles approach those of a constant magnetic field, with temperature inversion sustained by gravitational and collisional filtering. In the strongly collisional long-time-scale regime, field-induced anisotropy is nearly eliminated and individual loops remain approximately isotropic and isothermal; an increasing temperature profile emerges only after averaging over unresolved flux tubes of differing temperature.
AI.conclusion: Coulomb collisions largely suppress the macroscopic kinetic signatures of magnetic-field inhomogeneity in the transition region and low corona; observed temperature structure there reflects collisional filtering and the averaging of unresolved, individually near-isothermal flux tubes rather than collisionless anisotropy.

title: IMF-aware N-body forward modelling of membership selection functions for young open clusters
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables. Under revision at MNRAS
summary: We present an IMF-aware N-body forward-modelling framework, in which the stellar initial mass function (IMF) is an explicit input, to quantify the membership selection functions of open clusters, namely completeness and contamination as functions of magnitude. Accurate derivation of the IMF requires correcting for these selection effects, which otherwise distort the inferred present-day mass function. Our framework simulates clusters with IMF slopes $α_2 = -2.7, -2.3, -1.9$, converts them into synthetic Gaia observations, adds mock field populations, and recovers members with HDBSCAN to mimic observational membership selection. Applying this framework to 35 young open clusters (ages $\lesssim100$ Myr, distances $\lesssim600$ pc), we find declining completeness towards the faint limit; older, more expanded, and more diffuse models have lower completeness and higher contamination. For a given cluster, models with flatter IMFs yield modestly but systematically lower global completeness and higher contamination, despite initial cluster masses calibrated to the same observed member count. These models undergo more stellar evolution mass loss and expand more, resulting in lower projected stellar densities; their lower completeness is consistent with more diffuse clusters being harder to separate from field stars. Corrections derived from a mismatched IMF largely recover the total star counts but leave a larger distortion in the shape of the present-day luminosity function than those derived with the correct IMF. Because membership recovery is tied to a cluster's structural evolution and the specific membership algorithm used, our findings emphasize that selection functions should be inferred jointly with the IMF rather than assumed in advance.

AI.tldr: An IMF-aware N-body forward-modelling framework shows that open-cluster membership selection functions (completeness/contamination) depend on the assumed IMF, so selection functions and the IMF must be inferred jointly.
AI.motivation: Deriving the present-day mass function (and hence the IMF) from observed clusters requires correcting for membership selection effects (completeness and contamination as functions of magnitude); if left uncorrected these distort the inferred mass function. The authors argue selection functions are usually assumed rather than derived, and that membership recovery depends on cluster structure, so a framework linking the IMF to selection effects is needed.
AI.method: They build an IMF-aware N-body forward-modelling pipeline in which the stellar IMF is an explicit input. Clusters are simulated with IMF slopes α2 = -2.7, -2.3, -1.9, converted into synthetic Gaia observations, augmented with mock field populations, and members are recovered with HDBSCAN to mimic observational membership selection. The framework is applied to 35 young open clusters (ages ≲100 Myr, distances ≲600 pc), with initial masses calibrated to the same observed member count.
AI.result: Completeness declines toward the faint limit; older, more expanded, and more diffuse models show lower completeness and higher contamination. For a given cluster, flatter IMFs produce modestly but systematically lower global completeness and higher contamination, explained by greater stellar-evolution mass loss, more expansion, and lower projected stellar densities (more diffuse clusters are harder to separate from field stars). Corrections from a mismatched IMF largely recover total star counts but leave a larger distortion in the shape of the present-day luminosity function than corrections using the correct IMF.
AI.conclusion: Membership recovery is tied to a cluster's structural evolution and to the specific membership algorithm used. Therefore selection functions should be inferred jointly with the IMF rather than assumed in advance.

title: V347 Aurigae: from Peak to Quiescence
comment: accepted to PASP
summary: We present an analysis of eight epochs of high-resolution optical spectra of the YSO (young stellar object) V347 Aur. The source exhibits periodic brightness variations spanning $\sim$2 mag over several months, interpreted as cyclic accretion-burst and quiescent phases, making V347 Aur a useful probe of the broad range of accretion and outflow variability in YSOs. When faint, V347 Aur shows an M-type photospheric absorption spectrum; when bright, it exhibits a strong emission-line spectrum. Our Keck/HIRES spectroscopy was obtained during the decay of an accretion burst. The emission spectrum includes the strong H I, Ca II, and He I transitions commonly seen in YSOs, as well as numerous weaker metal lines, for which we provide a complete inventory. As the star fades, photospheric absorption lines deepen, consistent with decreasing veiling from the accretion continuum. H I and He I emission, which trace accretion, strengthen relative to the continuum as it fades, but show the expected decline in strength with decreasing accretion after correcting for the strong early veiling. Ca II behaves similarly, with line profiles that alternate between red- and blueshifted dominance, which we interpret as the rotation of the magnetospheric accretion flows. Narrow, slightly blueshifted absorption in Ca II, Na I, and K I indicates disk winds with localized density enhancements. Forbidden [O I] and [S II] emission is blueshifted, with broad shoulders and low- and high-velocity narrow peaks, consistent with a disk geometry that obscures much of the receding outflow. Their behavior as the continuum fades is similar to that of the broad accretion lines. The V347 Aur system is a useful proxy both for the ubiquitous short-term accretion variability observed in YSOs, and for their secular evolution on longer time scales.

AI.tldr: Analysis of eight Keck/HIRES epochs of V347 Aur during an accretion-burst decay reveals decreasing veiling, accretion-tracing H I/He I/Ca II emission that declines once veiling is corrected, rotating magnetospheric flows, disk-wind absorption, and blueshifted forbidden emission indicating an obscured receding outflow.
AI.motivation: V347 Aur shows periodic ~2 mag brightness variations over months, interpreted as cyclic accretion-burst and quiescent phases, making it a useful probe of the broad range of accretion and outflow variability in YSOs and a proxy for both short-term accretion variability and longer-term secular evolution.
AI.method: Eight epochs of high-resolution optical spectroscopy with Keck/HIRES obtained during the decay of an accretion burst; spectral inventory of emission and absorption features; tracking of veiling from the accretion continuum; analysis of line profiles (H I, He I, Ca II, Na I, K I) and forbidden [O I] and [S II] emission.
AI.result: Faint state shows an M-type photospheric absorption spectrum; bright state shows a strong emission-line spectrum including H I, Ca II, He I, and numerous weaker metal lines. As the star fades, photospheric absorption lines deepen (decreasing veiling). H I and He I emission strengthen relative to the fading continuum but decline in absolute strength with decreasing accretion after correcting for early veiling; Ca II behaves similarly with profiles alternating between red- and blueshifted dominance. Narrow, slightly blueshifted absorption in Ca II, Na I, and K I indicates disk winds with localized density enhancements. Forbidden [O I] and [S II] are blueshifted with broad shoulders and low-/high-velocity narrow peaks, consistent with a disk geometry obscuring much of the receding outflow, and behave similarly to the broad accretion lines as the continuum fades.
AI.conclusion: V347 Aur is a useful proxy for the ubiquitous short-term accretion variability observed in YSOs and for their secular evolution on longer time scales; its alternating Ca II profile dominance reflects rotation of magnetospheric accretion flows, and its forbidden-line asymmetry reflects an obscured receding outflow in a disk geometry.

title: Connecting galaxy structure, quenching, and halo environments during cosmic noon
comment: 21 pages, 12 figures, 4 tables
summary: The connection between galaxy structure, star formation activity, and large-scale environments provides important insights into the evolution of massive galaxies. However, the relative importance of different galaxy properties in predicting quenching and the environmental dependence of structurally distinct galaxy populations remain poorly constrained at cosmic noon ($1\leq z<3$). In this work, we investigate massive galaxies with $\log M_*/{\rm M}_{\odot}>10.5$ at $1\leq z<3$ using deep JWST/NIRCam imaging from the COSMOS-Web survey, combining measurements of central stellar mass surface density ($Σ_1$), star formation activity, and galaxy clustering. We find that $Σ_1$ is the most informative predictor of quenching among the considered properties, including stellar mass, effective radius, formation redshift, and local overdensity. The quenched fraction shows a strong dependence on $Σ_1$, increasing rapidly above a characteristic $Σ_1$. We further show that compact quenched galaxies exhibit a tendency toward stronger clustering than compact and extended star-forming galaxies, while compact and extended star-forming galaxies show similar clustering properties. These results highlight the importance of $Σ_1$ in tracing quenching and reveal that structural diversity among star-forming galaxies is not strongly reflected in their large-scale environments, providing new constraints on the interplay between galaxy structure, quenching, and halo environments during cosmic noon.

AI.motivation: The interplay between galaxy structure, star formation activity, and large-scale environment in driving quenching of massive galaxies is poorly constrained at cosmic noon (1≤z<3), particularly which galaxy property dominates quenching prediction and whether structurally distinct populations inhabit different environments.
AI.method: Deep JWST/NIRCam imaging from COSMOS-Web is used to study massive galaxies (log M*/M⊙>10.5) at 1≤z<3, combining measurements of central stellar mass surface density (Σ1), star formation activity, and galaxy clustering; Σ1 is compared against stellar mass, effective radius, formation redshift, and local overdensity as quenching predictors.
