AI.motivation: Dwarf galaxies form and evolve across diverse environments, but their study is hampered by resolution limitations and by systematic biases affecting their inferred properties. A comprehensive, multi-resolution numerical framework with observation-matching diagnostics is needed to interpret dwarf-galaxy formation in a cosmological context.
AI.method: RAMSES-based cosmological simulations with two components: DARWIN-1 (full box (65.5 cMpc)^3, 500 pc minimum cell) and DARWIN-2 (zoom-ins of 24 field regions and a Milky Way analog connected to a filament, 62.5 pc resolution). Baryonic physics is tailored per simulation; DARWIN-2 includes radiative transfer in three photon energy bands tracing hydrogen and helium ionization. Mock images are generated with SKIRT and Powderday, and a machine-learning approach is used to correct resolution-driven biases in DARWIN-1 dwarf properties using higher-resolution DARWIN-2 data.
AI.result: DARWIN-1 reproduces the cosmic SFR density and galaxy stellar mass functions reasonably well at z>1. Both simulations broadly reproduce observed stellar mass-halo mass relations, chemical abundances, star-formation surface densities, and black hole-galaxy scaling relations. At lower redshift, DARWIN-1 shows an excess in the number density of massive galaxies, though inferred stellar content depends on the galaxy stellar mass definition. Additional systematic differences arise from spatial resolution, feedback efficiency, and environmental selection.
AI.conclusion: The DARWIN suite offers a comprehensive numerical framework for studying dwarf-galaxy formation, evolution, and internal physics in a cosmological context, with built-in tools (mock imaging, ML-based resolution corrections) for quantitative comparison with observations.

title: Activity Cycles in Solar-Type Stars
comment: Accepted in Proc. IAUS 400
summary: Systematic observational studies, mainly focused on solar-type stars in the F to early K range, have detected magnetic activity cycles analogous to the solar one. When analyzing the relationship between the length of these cycles and stellar rotation rate, a non-monotonic dependence is observed. Activity periods are discretely distributed into two distinct branches: inactive and active. Intriguingly, some stars with rotation rates faster than the Sun exhibit two coexisting activity cycles, with periods simultaneously falling on both the inactive and active branches. In this work, we analyze the time series of the Mount Wilson index of a set of 44 stars, covering a range of rotation periods (sub-solar, solar, and super-solar), to identify single or double activity cycles. We detected activity cycles in 19 of the analyzed stars, with 7 of these exhibiting double-cycle behavior. In a complementary approach, we also analyze the activity cycles simulated for identical solar twins with rotation periods both shorter and longer than the Sun.

AI.tldr: Observationally derived activity cycles in 44 solar-type stars are examined to test the non-monotonic rotation–cycle relation, revealing single and double activity cycles, supplemented by simulated solar twins with varied rotation periods.
AI.motivation: Systematic studies of F to early K solar-type stars reveal magnetic activity cycles similar to the solar cycle, but the cycle length vs. rotation rate relation is non-monotonic, with cycle periods clustering into discrete inactive and active branches; some stars rotating faster than the Sun show two coexisting cycles spanning both branches. This motivates a dedicated search for single versus double cycles across sub-solar, solar, and super-solar rotators.
AI.method: Time-series analysis of the Mount Wilson S-index for a sample of 44 stars spanning sub-solar, solar, and super-solar rotation periods, to detect single or double activity cycles; complemented by analysis of simulated activity cycles for identical solar twins with rotation periods shorter and longer than the Sun.
AI.result: Activity cycles were detected in 19 of the analyzed stars, and 7 of these exhibit double-cycle behavior.
AI.conclusion: The occurrence of single and double activity cycles in the sample is consistent with the observed branching structure of activity periods; the combined observational and simulated solar-twin analyses provide a framework for interpreting double-cycle behavior in faster-than-solar rotators.

title: A high-Galactic-altitude scattering screen: scintillation from Globular Cluster pulsar M53A
summary: While known interstellar scattering screens are largely confined to the Galactic disk, the scattering properties of the circumgalactic medium (CGM) in the deep Galactic halo have remained unexplored. Using observations from the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), we report the first detection of scintillation arcs in the secondary spectra of the high-latitude pulsar J1312+1810A (M53A). Under the 1D anisotropic and 2D isotropic thin-screen models considered here, the inferred scintillation screen distances are $12.8_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.7_{-3.5}^{+2.8}$\,kpc, respectively. These model-dependent estimates correspond to Galactic heights of $12.6_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.5_{-3.5}^{+2.7}$\,kpc, placing the candidate screen among the highest-altitude scattering structures inferred to date. The strong, time-variable scintillation asymmetry suggests substantial electron-density inhomogeneity within the screen. We speculate that this screen is associated with small-scale structures near the shock boundary of the northern eROSITA bubble. These results support the presence of discrete, inhomogeneous scattering structures deep within the Galactic halo, far beyond the regions where localized stellar feedback is typically concentrated, and highlight pulsar scintillation as a promising probe of small-scale ionized structures in the CGM.

AI.tldr: Using FAST, the authors report the first detection of scintillation arcs in the secondary spectrum of high-latitude pulsar J1312+1810A (M53A), placing a scattering screen at ~11-13 kpc, among the highest-altitude screens known, and attribute it to small-scale structure near the northern eROSITA bubble shock boundary.
AI.motivation: Known interstellar scattering screens are mostly confined to the Galactic disk; the scattering properties of the circumgalactic medium in the deep Galactic halo remain unexplored.
AI.method: FAST observations of the high-latitude pulsar J1312+1810A (M53A) to detect scintillation arcs in its secondary spectrum, interpreting them with 1D anisotropic and 2D isotropic thin-screen models.
AI.result: Scintillation arcs detected for the first time in this pulsar's secondary spectrum. Inferred screen distances are 12.8_{-3.5}^{+2.6} kpc (1D anisotropic) and 11.7_{-3.5}^{+2.8} kpc (2D isotropic), corresponding to Galactic heights of 12.6_{-3.5}^{+2.6} and 11.5_{-3.5}^{+2.7} kpc. Strong, time-variable scintillation asymmetry indicates substantial electron-density inhomogeneity in the screen.
AI.conclusion: The results support discrete, inhomogeneous scattering structures deep in the Galactic halo, beyond typical stellar-feedback regions, and demonstrate pulsar scintillation as a promising probe of small-scale ionized structures in the CGM. The screen is tentatively linked to small-scale structures near the shock boundary of the northern eROSITA bubble.

title: Ultraviolet accretion continua reveal a transition in T Tauri magnetic topology
comment: Astrophysical Journal Letters, accepted (4 figures)
summary:
Magnetic fields regulate accretion in T Tauri stars (TTSs) and evolve as radiative cores emerge during pre-main-sequence contraction. Stars above ~0.35-0.5 Msun transition from fully convective to partially convective interiors, a change associated with increasingly complex magnetic topologies and evolving dynamo behaviour. Because accretion flows are magnetically channelled, this evolution is expected to modify ultraviolet (UV) accretion diagnostics, although observational evidence has remained limited.
  We identify a transition in the UV continuum properties of TTSs using archival International Ultraviolet Explorer observations, complemented by recent spectra from the Hubble Space Telescope ULLYSES survey. An empirical UV photospheric sequence constructed from G-M main-sequence stars shows that late K-M TTSs broadly follow standard photosphere-plus-shock model predictions, whereas G-K5 stars display systematically lower F270/F303 continuum flux ratios (flux at 270 nm relative to 303 nm).
  Statistical analysis shows that transition models describe the observations significantly better than a single continuous trend, locating the transition near spectral type K5-K6, with its precise location limited by spectral-classification uncertainties, and consistent with the fully convective boundary. Comparison with photosphere-plus-shock models further shows that, while the late-type population is broadly encompassed by the parameter space sampled by the adopted models, the warmer stars extend systematically beyond it in this UV diagnostic.
  We interpret this transition as evidence for a change in magnetospheric accretion associated with the evolution of magnetic topology across the radiative-core boundary, resulting in a corresponding change in the emergent UV continuum.

AI.tldr: Archival IUE plus HST ULLYSES UV spectra reveal a transition in T Tauri star UV continuum flux ratios near spectral type K5-K6, coinciding with the fully convective boundary, interpreted as a magnetic-topology-driven change in accretion.
AI.motivation: Magnetic fields govern accretion in T Tauri stars and evolve as radiative cores emerge; stars above ~0.35-0.5 Msun shift from fully to partially convective interiors, producing more complex magnetic topologies and altered dynamo behaviour. Since accretion is magnetically channelled, this should imprint on UV accretion diagnostics, but observational evidence has been limited.
AI.method: Analysis of archival International Ultraviolet Explorer observations complemented by HST ULLYSES spectra. An empirical UV photospheric sequence built from G-M main-sequence stars provides a reference; F270/F303 continuum flux ratios (270 nm relative to 303 nm) are compared with photosphere-plus-shock model predictions, and statistical model comparison tests a transition model against a single continuous trend.
AI.result: Late K-M TTSs broadly follow standard photosphere-plus-shock predictions, while G-K5 stars show systematically lower F270/F303 ratios. Transition models fit significantly better than a continuous trend, placing the transition near K5-K6 (limited by spectral-classification uncertainty) and consistent with the fully convective boundary. Warm stars extend systematically beyond the sampled model parameter space.
AI.conclusion: The observed UV continuum transition is interpreted as evidence for a change in magnetospheric accretion driven by magnetic-topology evolution across the radiative-core boundary, producing a corresponding change in emergent UV continuum emission.

title: The Solar System through dust maps. Encounter statistics with interstellar gas
summary: During its orbit around the Milky Way, the Solar System crosses different environments, including dense ISM regions. These encounters increase dust influx, leave geological signatures, and affect the heliosphere. For the local ISM, we estimate crossing frequencies and durations, the fraction of time spent above gas density thresholds, and how Solar vertical motion and ISM stratification influence these statistics. We quantify gas influx and dust exposure. We use Gaia-based 3D dust maps of the Solar neighborhood, sampled by integrating the Solar System along its Galactic orbit while rigidly translating the maps. From the resulting density time series, encounter statistics and fluxes are derived. We find that the Solar System spends most of its time in low density environments, while crossings of dense gas become rarer with increasing density threshold. For nH>=1cm^-3, the crossing frequency is above 600Gyr^-1, whereas thresholds around 200cm^-3 are crossed once per Gyr. Individual crossings last tens of kyr and become shorter at higher density thresholds. The inferred durations soon become nearly constant, reflecting the finite spatial resolution of the maps. The Sun spends 18 to 47% of the sampled time above 1cm^-3, and 1 to 10% above 10cm^-3. The residence fraction can be reproduced by combining the vertical volume filling factor of gas with the fraction of time spent by the Sun at each height. Within the current vertical range sampled by the Sun, we find no clear enhancement of crossing statistics during midplane passages, suggesting that these do not necessarily lead to periodic perturbations of the Solar System. About 50% of the gas influx is contributed by gas with nH<=3-4cm^-3, and about 90% by gas with nH<=48cm^-3. Our results provide a first order, data driven estimate of ISM encounter statistics, gas influx, and dust exposure along the Solar System's Galactic orbit.

AI.tldr: Using Gaia-based 3D dust maps sampled along the Solar System's Galactic orbit, this study quantifies how often and how long the Sun encounters dense interstellar medium, and estimates the associated gas influx and dust exposure.
AI.motivation: As the Solar System orbits the Milky Way it traverses diverse ISM environments, including dense regions that raise dust influx, leave geological signatures, and perturb the heliosphere. A data-driven characterization of these encounters and their statistics is needed.
AI.method: Gaia-based 3D dust maps of the Solar neighborhood are sampled by integrating the Solar System along its Galactic orbit while rigidly translating the maps, producing density time series from which crossing frequencies, durations, residence fractions above density thresholds, gas influx, and dust exposure are derived. The influence of Solar vertical motion and ISM stratification is also examined.
AI.result: Most time is spent in low-density environments; crossings become rarer with higher thresholds (frequency >600 Gyr^-1 for nH>=1 cm^-3, ~1 Gyr^-1 near 200 cm^-3). Individual crossings last tens of kyr and shorten at higher thresholds until limited by map resolution. The Sun spends 18–47% of sampled time above 1 cm^-3 and 1–10% above 10 cm^-3. Residence fractions are reproduced by combining the vertical volume filling factor with the time spent at each height. No clear enhancement during midplane passages is found. About 50% of gas influx comes from nH<=3–4 cm^-3 and ~90% from nH<=48 cm^-3.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a first-order, data-driven estimate of ISM encounter statistics, gas influx, and dust exposure along the Solar System's Galactic orbit.

title: Reading Between the Lines: How Much Information Remains After Fitting a Stellar Spectrum?
comment: 21 pages, 14 figures; submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics; code at https://github.com/svenbuder/residual_cannon; comments welcome
summary: What if we could model 100% of a stellar spectrum? Modern surveys infer stellar properties by comparing observed spectra with synthetic models, yet even the best fits leave structured residuals. We analyse 7087 GALAH survey spectra and ask what information remains after subtracting each best-fitting model. Across 13927 pixels, 4.5% of residuals exceed $3σ$, far above 0.3% expected from Gaussian noise. We map the amplitude, significance, sign, and recurrence of these residuals and identify 380 significant regions. Comparison with stellar atlases, line lists, diffuse interstellar bands, and sky diagnostics links most regions to plausible causes: 62% are candidate line-strength or line-profile mismatches, while others trace missing or unidentified lines, interstellar absorption, sky emission, or broader reduction structure. We then train data-driven models on the residual spectra themselves. Residual-only models recover $T_\mathrm{eff}$ to 80-150 K and [Fe/H] to 0.059-0.086 dex, depending on sample quality, and retain weaker, partly indirect information about elemental abundances. Extinction-related coefficients recover the strongest known interstellar features, whereas chromospheric activity leaves plausible Balmer-line signatures but is not recovered robustly out of sample. Most strikingly, the residual flux in 6% of wavelength pixels that were synthesised but excluded from the GALAH DR4 optimisation recovers stellar labels almost as well as the full residual spectrum and better than the remaining 94% alone. Residuals are therefore not merely imperfections to discard: they map missing line data, incomplete physics, unfitted astrophysical components, and observational systematics. Reading between the lines turns one spectroscopist's trash into another one's treasure, and provides a practical route towards extracting more of the information already present in stellar spectra.

AI.tldr: The authors analyze structured residuals from 7,087 GALAH spectra after subtracting best-fitting synthetic models, map 380 significant residual regions to physical causes, and show that the residual spectra alone retain recoverable stellar-label information, including strong signal in synthesis-only pixels.
AI.motivation: Model-based spectroscopic surveys infer stellar properties by fitting synthetic spectra, but best fits leave structured residual patterns that are usually discarded. The paper asks whether this leftover information is useless noise or a source of physical and diagnostic signal.
AI.method: They examine residuals of 7,087 GALAH spectra across 13,927 pixels following best-model subtraction, quantify their statistical excess, map amplitude, significance, sign, and recurrence to identify 380 significant regions, cross-match these with stellar atlases, line lists, diffuse interstellar bands, and sky diagnostics, and train data-driven models on residual spectra to test label recovery.
AI.result: 4.5% of residuals exceed 3σ versus 0.3% expected from Gaussian noise; 62% of significant regions are candidate line-strength or line-profile mismatches, with others tracing unidentified lines, interstellar absorption, sky emission, or reduction structure. Residual-only models recover T_eff to 80-150 K and [Fe/H] to 0.059-0.086 dex with weaker indirect abundance information; extinction coefficients recover strong interstellar features, while chromospheric activity is not robust out of sample. Residual flux in the 6% of synthesis-only pixels excluded from DR4 optimisation recovers labels almost as well as the full residual spectrum.
AI.conclusion: Residuals are informative rather than disposable: they diagnose missing line data, incomplete physics, unfitted astrophysical components, and observational systematics, and offer a practical route to extracting additional information already present in stellar spectra.

title: Effect of galaxy mergers on dust masses
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables, 3 appendices, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Dust mass (M$_{Dust}$) is one of the key physical properties of galaxies that track the cold interstellar medium. However, the M$_{Dust}$ in merging galaxies is poorly understood. We aim to derive how the cold dust mass of galaxies is affected by major mergers at low redshifts. M$_{Dust}$ was estimated for approximately 500 major mergers in the North Ecliptic Pole extragalactic field using spectral energy distribution fitting runs with CIGALE, with different dust attenuation and emission models. We also analysed over 12 000 mergers from the SIMBA simulation using its M$_{Dust}$. We matched merging and non-merging systems in stellar mass, redshift, and local density, to enable a comparison of M$_{Dust}$. We then performed a second comparison using a control sample also matched in SFR. AGN host galaxies were then removed, and this matching repeated. Observed mergers have larger M$_{Dust}$ than the non-mergers by up to a factor of 1.82$\pm$0.35, or 1.60$\pm$0.44 without AGN-hosts. When matched by SFR, observed mergers show no significant change in M$_{Dust}$, both when including and excluding AGN-hosts. SIMBA galaxies show similar trends when AGN-hosts are included but there is still an increase in M$_{Dust}$ when matched by SFR. When AGN-hosts are excluded, the SIMBA mergers show smaller M$_{Dust}$ by a factor of 0.98$\pm$0.03, or 0.97$\pm$0.02 when matched in SFR. The higher the mass of a merger, the greater M$_{Dust}$ increase for observations for two of the CIGALE runs, or the smaller the decrease for SIMBA. Observed mergers are typically more dusty than their non-merging counterparts but only because they typically have higher SFRs, regardless of whether they host AGN or not. SIMBA mergers follow observations when AGN hosts are included, but show reduced M$_{Dust}$ when AGN hosts are removed. M$_{Dust}$ in SIMBA is linked to AGN in a way not seen in observations.

AI.tldr: Low-redshift observed major mergers have up to ~1.6–1.8× higher dust mass than non-mergers, but this excess disappears once matched in SFR; SIMBA reproduces this trend for AGN hosts but predicts reduced dust mass for mergers without AGN.
AI.motivation: Dust mass (M_Dust) traces the cold interstellar medium, yet how major mergers at low redshift affect galactic cold dust mass remains poorly understood.
AI.method: M_Dust was derived for ~500 NEP-field major mergers via CIGALE SED fitting with multiple dust attenuation/emission models, and for >12,000 SIMBA simulation mergers. Merging and non-merging systems were matched in stellar mass, redshift, and local density, then additionally in SFR, with the matching repeated after removing AGN hosts.
AI.result: Observed mergers show higher M_Dust than non-mergers by 1.82±0.35 (1.60±0.44 excluding AGN hosts), but no significant change once matched in SFR. SIMBA matches observations with AGN hosts included but yields 0.98±0.03 (0.97±0.02 SFR-matched) for mergers without AGN hosts. Dust excess grows (observations) or deficit shrinks (SIMBA) with merger mass.
AI.conclusion: Observed mergers are dustier than non-mergers only because of their higher SFRs, independent of AGN presence; SIMBA reproduces observations only with AGN hosts, implying an AGN–dust coupling in the simulation absent in observations.

title: Gravity-mode main-sequence asteroseismology of 16 open clusters and associations
comment: 26 pages, 16 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJS
summary: Coeval stellar populations offer a unique advantage for studying stellar physics because their members share a common age and broadly similar initial chemical composition, allowing the free parameters in stellar models to be constrained more efficiently. Meanwhile, asteroseismology, through the study of pulsation modes that propagate through stellar interiors, provides powerful constraints on internal structure and the physical processes operating beneath stellar atmospheres. The combination of coeval-population studies and asteroseismology therefore provides an unparalleled laboratory for testing and improving stellar evolutionary and structural models. Using light curves from the Kepler and TESS space missions, together with membership constraints based on Gaia astrometry, we identify g-mode period-spacing patterns in dozens of early-type ($T_{\rm eff} \gtrsim 7000\,\mathrm{K}$) main-sequence stars across 16 stellar groups. From these patterns, we infer near-core rotation rates $f_\mathrm{rot}$ and measure the asymptotic spacing $Π_0$ of g modes, tracing both angular-momentum transport and the evolution of the convective stellar cores. Using our homogeneous set of g-mode stellar-group members spanning a wide range of ages, we show that near-core rotation in early-type stars decreases with stellar evolution. We compare our results with existing model predictions. Our $Π_0$ measurements still show discrepancies with current stellar models for reasons that remain unclear, as reported in several previous studies. We also report two g-mode pre-main-sequence pulsators and three pulsating blue stragglers. Our sample provides a useful basis for calibrating stellar models in future ensemble asteroseismic studies of coeval stellar populations.

AI.tldr: By combining Kepler/TESS light curves with Gaia astrometry to find g-mode period-spacing patterns in early-type main-sequence members of 16 coeval stellar groups, the authors measure near-core rotation rates and asymptotic g-mode spacings, showing that near-core rotation declines with stellar evolution and that Π0 still disagrees with current models.
AI.motivation: Coeval stellar populations share age and initial composition, greatly reducing free parameters in stellar models, while asteroseismology probes internal structure and physics beneath the atmosphere. Combining the two offers a powerful laboratory for testing stellar evolutionary and structural models, particularly for angular-momentum transport and convective-core evolution in early-type stars.
AI.method: Uses Kepler and TESS light curves together with Gaia-astrometry-based membership constraints to identify g-mode period-spacing patterns in dozens of early-type (Teff ≳ 7000 K) main-sequence stars across 16 stellar groups. From these patterns the near-core rotation rate f_rot and asymptotic g-mode spacing Π0 are inferred, tracing angular-momentum transport and convective-core evolution in a homogeneous sample spanning a wide age range.
AI.result: Near-core rotation in early-type stars is found to decrease with stellar evolution, and the results are compared with existing model predictions. Π0 measurements still show discrepancies with current stellar models for reasons that remain unclear, consistent with several previous studies. Two g-mode pre-main-sequence pulsators and three pulsating blue stragglers are also reported.
AI.conclusion: The homogeneous set of g-mode stellar-group members provides a useful basis for calibrating stellar models in future ensemble asteroseismic studies of coeval stellar populations, while highlighting unresolved tensions in Π0 predictions.

title: The Central Molecular Zone of our Galaxy, a chemical complexity factory: first interstellar detections of molecules towards G+0.693
comment: Part of "Traversing the Galactic Center in Space and Time Proceedings IAU Symposium No. 405", M. Zajaček, T. Jerábková, V. Karas, R. Schödel & P. Suková, eds
summary: The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of our Galaxy is a prime laboratory for interstellar chemistry because of its extreme conditions, such as shocks and high cosmic-ray ionisation rates. It is an efficient factory of molecules, with many species first discovered in CMZ sources. This document reviews key results from the study of the CMZ G+0.693-0.027 molecular cloud. Using ultra-sensitive broadband spectral surveys together with laboratory spectroscopy, more than 140 molecules have been identified, including 28 detected for the first time in the interstellar medium (ISM). These discoveries include prebiotic precursors of biomolecules, increasingly complex members of known molecular families, molecules containing periodic third-row elements (S, P, Na, Mg), high-energy stereo- and structural isomers, and new cations. Overall, these findings extend the known limits of interstellar chemical complexity and highlight the CMZ's potential to provide the molecular ingredients for prebiotic chemistry.

AI.tldr: A review of the CMZ cloud G+0.693-0.027 reporting >140 molecules identified, 28 of them new to the ISM, covering prebiotic precursors, third-row element species, isomers, and cations, extending the limits of interstellar chemical complexity.
AI.motivation: The CMZ offers extreme conditions (shocks, high cosmic-ray ionization rates) making it an efficient molecular factory and a prime laboratory for interstellar chemistry; many species were first discovered in CMZ sources, motivating a synthesis of results from the G+0.693-0.027 cloud.
AI.method: Ultra-sensitive broadband spectral surveys of G+0.693-0.027 combined with laboratory spectroscopy for line identification and confirmation.
AI.result: More than 140 molecules identified, including 28 detected for the first time in the ISM; discoveries span prebiotic precursors of biomolecules, increasingly complex members of known molecular families, molecules with periodic third-row elements (S, P, Na, Mg), high-energy stereo- and structural isomers, and new cations.
AI.conclusion: These findings extend the known limits of interstellar chemical complexity and highlight the CMZ's potential to supply the molecular ingredients for prebiotic chemistry.

title: Kinematic structure and age of a Scorpius--Centaurus subcomponent: implications for PDS 70 planetary system
comment: 25 pages, 25 figures, submitted to MNRAS. Comments are welcome! Related data (and near future: related code) can be accessed at https://github.com/aruuniima/T-subcomponent_PDS70 and the Chronostar code is publicly available at https://github.com/tcrundall/chronostar-tng
summary: PDS~70, the only system with two directly imaged protoplanets embedded in their natal disk, is a benchmark for giant-planet formation theory. Interpreting the planetary luminosities requires a precise age for the host star, but the widely adopted isochronal age of $5.4\pm1.0$~Myr is substantially younger than ages inferred for the Upper Centaurus--Lupus (UCL) population with which it is associated. We address this discrepancy by determining a new kinematic age for PDS~70 using radial velocities for 405 candidate members of the Scorpius--Centaurus T subcomponent from the Wide Field Spectrograph (WiFeS) on the ANU 2.3~m telescope, reducing uncertainties by a factor of $\sim5.5$ compared to \textit{Gaia}. %We supplement these measurements with H$α$ and lithium equivalent widths as youth diagnostics. We combine these with \textit{Gaia} DR3 astrometry in the \texttt{Chronostar} kinematic reconstruction framework to derive a posterior-weighted kinematic age of approximately $10$--$15$~Myr for all the T subcomponent stars, with a kinematic age of $\approx 12$--$16$~Myr for PDS 70, ruling out ages as young as the published isochronal estimate. At this kinematic age, PDS~70~\textit{b}'s (and to a lesser extent, PDS~70~\textit{c}'s) luminosity is incompatible with warm-start cooling tracks under current dynamical mass constraints. The most natural interpretation is that PDS~70~\textit{b} formed $\approx10.5$ Myr after its host star, and no less than $\approx7.7$ Myr after it.

AI.tldr: A new kinematic age of ~10–15 Myr for PDS 70 (≈12–16 Myr for the star itself), based on 405 WiFeS radial velocities combined with Gaia DR3 astrometry in Chronostar, rules out the young 5.4 Myr isochronal age and implies PDS 70 b formed ~10.5 Myr after its host star.
AI.motivation: PDS 70 hosts the only two directly imaged protoplanets still embedded in their natal disk, making it a benchmark for giant-planet formation. Interpreting the planets' luminosities requires an accurate host-star age, but the widely used isochronal age of 5.4±1.0 Myr is much younger than ages inferred for the associated Upper Centaurus–Lupus (UCL)/Scorpius–Centaurus population, creating a discrepancy that undermines luminosity-based mass and formation-time inferences.
AI.method: Radial velocities for 405 candidate members of the Scorpius–Centaurus T subcomponent were measured with the WiFeS spectrograph on the ANU 2.3 m telescope, reducing velocity uncertainties by a factor of ~5.5 relative to Gaia. These data were combined with Gaia DR3 astrometry within the Chronostar kinematic reconstruction framework to derive posterior-weighted kinematic ages for the T subcomponent and for PDS 70 specifically.
AI.result: The kinematic age of the T subcomponent population is ~10–15 Myr, with ≈12–16 Myr for PDS 70 itself, confidently excluding ages as young as the published isochronal value. At this older age, PDS 70 b's luminosity (and, less strongly, PDS 70 c's) is incompatible with warm-start cooling tracks given current dynamical mass constraints.
AI.conclusion: The most natural interpretation is that PDS 70 b formed ≈10.5 Myr after its host star, and no less than ≈7.7 Myr after it, implying a substantially delayed formation epoch relative to the star and challenging standard core-accretion timescales under warm-start assumptions.

title: The Milky Way's Early Disk Was Built in Bursts. I. Evidence from Low-angular-momentum, High-$α$ Stars Scattered Out of the Protodisk by Merger Events
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures, Published in AJ
summary: Stars born in the high-$α$ disk can later acquire low angular momentum through dynamical scattering during early merger events. Their age--metallicity distribution thus provides a fossil record of the history of both star formation and dynamical perturbations in the early Milky Way disk. Here we identify a sample of 2,078 such stars from more than two million Gaia DR3 subgiants with robust determinations of ages, kinematics, and abundances. From this sample we reconstruct their intrinsic age--metallicity distribution with a forward modeling approach. Our results confirm that these scattered stars are older and more metal-poor than the bulk of the high-$α$ disk on average. In particular, the joint age--metallicity distribution reveals a robust two-component feature: a broad, dominant component with a peak age of $\sim$11.5~Gyr and ${\rm [Fe/H]}\simeq-0.59$, and an older and more metal-poor component with a peak age of $\sim$12.5~Gyr and ${\rm [Fe/H]}\simeq-0.86$. The presence of this two-component structure suggests that the high-$α$ disk experienced episodic phases of star formation and chemical enrichment. The age distribution of the younger Splash component, compared with that of the high-$α$ disk, provides evidence for a substantial dynamical perturbation at a lookback time of 10.8--11.5~Gyr, possibly associated with an early passage of Gaia--Sausage--Enceladus (GSE). The older Splash component, with a peak age of $\sim$12.5~Gyr, may preserve signatures of an earlier interaction, possibly associated with the proposed Low-energy--Kraken--Heracles (LKH) event.

AI.tldr: A sample of 2,078 scattered low-angular-momentum "Splash" subgiants, selected from >2 million Gaia DR3 subgiants with reliable ages, kinematics and abundances, shows a bimodal age–metallicity distribution indicating episodic star formation and two distinct dynamical perturbation events in the early Milky Way disk.
AI.motivation: Stars formed in the high-alpha disk can be driven to low angular momentum by dynamical scattering during early mergers, so their age–metallicity distribution encodes the joint history of early disk star formation and dynamical heating. The authors aim to reconstruct this fossil record to identify the timing of early perturbation events.
AI.method: Selection of 2,078 low-angular-momentum high-alpha stars from over two million Gaia DR3 subgiants with robust ages, kinematics and chemical abundances; reconstruction of the intrinsic age–metallicity distribution via forward modeling to correct for selection and observational effects.
AI.result: The scattered stars are confirmed to be older and more metal-poor than the bulk high-alpha disk. The joint age–metallicity distribution shows a robust two-component structure: a dominant broad component peaking at ~11.5 Gyr with [Fe/H] ≈ -0.59, and an older, more metal-poor component peaking at ~12.5 Gyr with [Fe/H] ≈ -0.86.
AI.conclusion: The two-component structure points to episodic phases of star formation and chemical enrichment in the high-alpha disk. The younger Splash component indicates a substantial dynamical perturbation at lookback times of 10.8–11.5 Gyr, plausibly an early Gaia–Sausage–Enceladus passage; the older component (~12.5 Gyr) may preserve signatures of an earlier interaction, possibly the proposed Low-energy–Kraken–Heracles event.

title: Competitive roles of turbulence and magnetic field on the formation of unipolar outflows in isolated molecular cloud cores
comment: Accepted for publication in PASJ
summary: We investigate the impact of turbulence and magnetic field on the formation of unipolar outflows in the gravitational collapse of isolated low-mass cloud cores using three-dimensional non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics simulations. In the models explored in this study, we find that unipolar outflows are formed in cloud cores with the super-Alfvénic turbulence of $M_{\rm{A}}>1$, where $M_{\rm{A}}$ is the Alfvén Mach number of the initial cloud core. In contrast, bipolar outflows are formed in cloud cores with $M_{\rm{A}}\lesssim1$. Our results suggest that the relative strength of the turbulence to the magnetic field in the initial cloud core plays a key role in the formation of unipolar outflows. We also find that no outflow is formed in cloud cores with the strong magnetic field of the dimensionless mass-to-flux ratio $μ=2$. The outflow morphologies can be used as tracers to indirectly estimate the relative strengths of the turbulence and magnetic field of the parent cloud cores.

AI.tldr: Using 3D non-ideal MHD simulations, the authors show that unipolar outflows form in isolated low-mass cloud cores with super-Alfvénic turbulence (M_A > 1), bipolar outflows form with M_A ≲ 1, and no outflows form under strong magnetic fields (μ = 2); outflow morphology thus traces the turbulence-to-field ratio of the parent core.
AI.motivation: Unipolar outflows are observed but their formation conditions are poorly understood. This work asks what role the relative strength of turbulence versus magnetic field in the initial cloud core plays in determining whether a unipolar, bipolar, or no outflow emerges.
AI.method: Three-dimensional non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics simulations of the gravitational collapse of isolated low-mass cloud cores, varying the initial Alfvén Mach number M_A (turbulence strength) and the dimensionless mass-to-flux ratio μ (field strength).
AI.result: Unipolar outflows form for M_A > 1 (super-Alfvénic turbulence); bipolar outflows form for M_A ≲ 1; no outflow forms for strong fields with μ = 2.
AI.conclusion: The turbulence-to-magnetic-field ratio in the initial core governs outflow type. Outflow morphology can serve as a tracer to indirectly estimate the relative turbulence and field strengths of parent cloud cores.

title: Star formation history of Draco revealed by DESI DR1: suppressed early star formation efficiency for Milky Way dwarf galaxies
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Dwarf galaxies serve as fossils for understanding the early star formation history of the local Universe. In this work, we use stellar abundances for individual stars derived from the first data release of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI DR1) to investigate the star formation history of the dwarf spheroidal galaxy Draco. We simultaneously fit the stellar metallicity distribution function (MDF) and the [Mg/Fe]-[Fe/H] trend using the galactic chemical evolution (GCE) model flexCE. Our best-fit models imply a low star formation efficiency (SFE) of $0.003$ to $0.007\,\mathrm{Gyr}^{-1}$, which is about ten times lower than values reported in the literature, but consistent with recent SFE estimates for ultra-faint dwarf galaxies. By combining recent literature measurements, we find that the SFEs of Milky Way dwarf galaxies scale with stellar mass as $\mathrm{SFE}\propto M_\star^{0.24}$. A low star formation efficiency is associated with a strong outflow efficiency; we estimate a large wind mass-loading factor $η_{\mathrm{wind}}$ of approximately 172-260. This is well in line with the observed outflow-stellar mass relation and with the Feedback in Realistic Environment (FIRE) cosmological simulations. Our results demonstrate the power of large-scale, low-to-medium resolution stellar spectroscopic surveys to deliver robust constraints on the early formation history of galaxies in the local Universe.

AI.tldr: Using DESI DR1 stellar abundances, the authors fit the metallicity distribution function and [Mg/Fe]-[Fe/H] trend of the Draco dwarf spheroidal with the flexCE chemical evolution model, deriving a low star formation efficiency and large wind mass-loading factor, and establishing an SFE-stellar mass scaling relation.
AI.motivation: Dwarf galaxies are fossils of early star formation in the local Universe, so constraining their star formation history informs early galaxy formation. Large spectroscopic surveys like DESI now provide individual stellar abundances that enable robust chemical-evolution modeling of these systems.
AI.method: The authors use stellar abundances for individual stars from DESI Data Release 1 and simultaneously fit the metallicity distribution function (MDF) and the [Mg/Fe]-[Fe/H] trend of the Draco dwarf spheroidal galaxy using the galactic chemical evolution model flexCE. They also combine their results with literature measurements to examine scaling relations.
AI.result: Best-fit models yield a low star formation efficiency of 0.003-0.007 per Gyr, roughly ten times lower than literature values but consistent with recent estimates for ultra-faint dwarfs. Combining with literature, the SFE of Milky Way dwarf galaxies scales as SFE proportional to M_star^0.24. The low SFE implies strong outflows with a wind mass-loading factor of about 172-260, consistent with observed outflow-stellar mass relations and FIRE cosmological simulations.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale, low-to-medium resolution stellar spectroscopic surveys can deliver robust constraints on the early formation history of local Universe galaxies. The results highlight the close connection between low star formation efficiency and strong feedback-driven outflows in dwarf galaxies.

title: Disc breaking and parametric instability in warped accretion discs driven by differential precession
comment: Submitted to MNRAS
summary: We present the first local simulations of accretion disc breaking (or disc tearing) with differential precession. Precession can occur due to a non-spherical potential (e.g. tilted circumbinary discs), or relativistic effects (e.g. tilted discs around spinning black holes). This tends to induce a twist in the disc, potentially causing it to break into rings. We extend earlier work on free (unforced) warps in Held+2026 [arXiv:2511.18655v1] to include differential precession in the shearing box, and carry out quasi-2D, isothermal, high-resolution ($N = 32$ cells per scale-height $H$) numerical simulations in which an imposed precession drives a warp in a tilted disc in either the wavelike ($α< H/r$) or diffusive ($α> H/r$) regime. Our key finding is that, at sufficiently large tilts and precession amplitudes, the disc breaks into multiple (4-5) mutually tilted rings exhibiting a rich morphology: from wide ($\sim 10H$), flat rings to compact tori of width $\sim H$. Interactions between rings occur as a result of oblique shocks that form in the gaps between them, leading to instances of disc rejoining. Smaller tilts and precession amplitudes lead instead to parametric instability of inertial waves in the disc. We develop a linear viscous theory of bending waves under the influence of an imposed precession. Finally, we present a systematic study of the effects of grid-based dissipation on tilted discs, and find that numerical dissipation damps the tilt and induces precession. This effect decreases with resolution as $\propto (1/N)^β$, $2.3 \lesssim β\lesssim 3.9$.

AI.tldr: First local (shearing-box) simulations of accretion disc breaking with differential precession, showing that large tilts/precession amplitudes fragment the disc into multiple tilted rings via oblique shocks, while small tilts trigger parametric instability of inertial waves.
AI.motivation: Differential precession—arising from non-spherical potentials (e.g. tilted circumbinary discs) or relativistic effects (e.g. tilted discs around spinning black holes)—twists a disc and can break it into rings ("disc tearing"). Earlier local work on free warps (Held+2026) lacked differential precession, so a local model incorporating forced precession was needed to study breaking dynamics.
AI.method: Quasi-2D, isothermal, high-resolution shearing-box simulations (N = 32 cells per scale height H) with an imposed differential precession driving a warp in a tilted disc, covering both the wavelike (α < H/r) and diffusive (α > H/r) regimes. Includes a linear viscous theory of bending waves under imposed precession and a systematic study of grid-based numerical dissipation on tilted discs.
AI.result: At sufficiently large tilts and precession amplitudes, the disc breaks into multiple (4–5) mutually tilted rings spanning wide, flat rings (~10H) to compact tori (~H width). Oblique shocks form in the gaps and mediate ring interactions, including instances of disc rejoining. Smaller tilts/amplitudes instead produce parametric instability of inertial waves. Numerical dissipation damps tilt and induces precession, scaling as ∝(1/N)^β with 2.3 ≲ β ≲ 3.9.
AI.conclusion: Differential precession in a local shearing-box model reproduces disc breaking into multiple tilted rings with rich morphology and shock-mediated interactions, distinguishing a breaking regime from a parametric-instability regime. Numerical dissipation on tilted discs converges slowly (β ≈ 2.3–3.9), an important caveat for grid-based warp studies.

title: PRISMS/U13151. A Glimpse into the Earliest Phases of Galaxy Formation through an Ultra-Faint System $\approx$ 500 Myr after the Big Bang
comment: 37 pages, 15 plots, 3 tables. Submitted to ApJ. Comments are welcome!
summary: Detailed UV-to-optical studies of galaxies at z >= 10 have largely focused on bright systems (MUV <= -20 mag), leaving intrinsically faint galaxies virtually unexplored to date. Combining NIRCam, NIRSpec, and MIRI imaging and spectroscopy, we investigate UNCOVER-ABELL2744-13151 (U13151), an ultra-faint galaxy at z = 9.7995 (MUV = -17.44 mag), magnified by Abell 2744 ($μ$ = 12.8). U13151 is very blue ($β$ ~ -2.64), ultra-low mass (log10(M*/Msun) ~ 6.68), young (~ 5.5 Myr), metal-poor (Z ~ 3-6% Zsun), and compact (Re ~ 122 pc). It exhibits negligible dust attenuation, extreme ionization conditions, and intense star formation (sSFR(Ha) ~ 94 Gyr-1, or equivalently M*/SFR(Ha) ~ 10.6 Myr). Despite similarities with much brighter galaxies, its low C/O, approximately solar Ne/O, and undetected nitrogen emission suggest enrichment dominated by core-collapse supernovae, in stark contrast with similar nitrogen-enhanced systems. U13151 might be undergoing its first major episode of star formation, assembling most (if not all) of its M* through five unresolved clumps. Its high ionizing photon production efficiency (log10($ξ_{\rm ion}$/ (Hz erg-1)) ~ 25.64) suggests, through a simple toy model, suggests, through a simple toy model, that similarly short-lived episodes could contribute significantly to the ionizing photon budget of low-mass galaxies during Cosmic Reionization. We explore different evolutionary scenarios, from U13151-like galaxies potentially representing the progenitors of Blue Monsters at higher redshifts to the possibility that such systems could be the early building blocks of present-day Milky Way-like galaxies. Our results highlight the fundamental role of MIRI in studying galaxies in the early Universe and the urgent need to investigate the faintest, lowest-mass systems to shed light on the fundamental physics driving the earliest phases of galaxy formation.

AI.tldr: U13151 is an ultra-faint (MUV = -17.44), extremely young, metal-poor, low-mass galaxy at z = 9.7995, revealed through NIRCam/NIRSpec/MIRI observations under strong lensing magnification. Its chemistry points to core-collapse supernova enrichment, and its high ionizing efficiency suggests short starburst episodes in low-mass galaxies could substantially power Cosmic Reionization.
AI.motivation: UV-to-optical studies at z >= 10 have concentrated on bright systems (MUV <= -20), leaving intrinsically faint, low-mass galaxies essentially unexplored. The authors aim to characterize such a system to probe the earliest phases of galaxy formation and the ionizing budget during Cosmic Reionization.
AI.method: Combined NIRCam imaging, NIRSpec and MIRI spectroscopy of the lensed ultra-faint galaxy UNCOVER-ABELL2744-13151 (U13151) at z = 9.7995, magnified by Abell 2744 (mu = 12.8). Derived stellar mass, age, metallicity, size, dust, UV slope, ionization conditions, and emission-line abundances (C/O, Ne/O, N); a toy model links ionizing photon production efficiency to the reionization photon budget.
AI.result: U13151 is very blue (beta ~ -2.64), ultra-low mass (log M*/Msun ~ 6.68), young (~5.5 Myr), metal-poor (Z ~ 3-6% Zsun), compact (Re ~ 122 pc), with negligible dust, extreme ionization, and intense star formation (sSFR(Ha) ~ 94 Gyr^-1; M*/SFR ~ 10.6 Myr). Low C/O, near-solar Ne/O, and undetected N emission indicate core-collapse-supernova-dominated enrichment. Star formation appears concentrated in five unresolved clumps, likely a first major burst. High ionizing efficiency (log xi_ion ~ 25.64) implies short-lived episodes can contribute significantly to the ionizing photon budget of low-mass galaxies.
AI.conclusion: U13151 may be assembling most of its stellar mass in a first major starburst, possibly a progenitor of Blue Monsters at higher redshift or an early building block of Milky Way-like galaxies. The work underscores MIRI's essential role and the urgency of studying the faintest, lowest-mass systems to understand early galaxy formation physics.

title: Kinematics and Thermodynamics of Coronal Mass Ejections
comment: PhD Thesis, Indian Institute of Astrophysics & Pondicherry University, 271 pages, Contributing papers have been published independently in ApJ, A&A, MNRAS and JAA journals
summary: Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are major drivers of space weather, yet their thermodynamic evolution remains insufficiently constrained. This thesis develops a comprehensive framework linking CME kinematics, thermodynamics, internal force balance, and geoeffectiveness through analytical modelling and multi-viewpoint observations. The developed FRIS model uses observed kinematics to infer otherwise inaccessible internal plasma properties, including the polytropic index. A systematic investigation of fast CMEs reveals an initial heat-release phase followed by a transition towards near-isothermal evolution, typically around 3-9 solar radii. The evolving contributions of thermal-pressure and centrifugal forces, opposed by the Lorentz force, establish a connection between expansion and thermal evolution. The findings demonstrate the limitations of assuming a fixed polytropic index in magnetohydrodynamic models of CME propagation. At 1 au, in situ observations reveal persistent non-adiabatic evolution, accompanied by turbulence and localised intermittency. The interacting CMEs associated with the May 2024 great storm show restructured magnetic and thermal configurations, producing double-flux-rope-like signatures and species-dependent heating, with electron thermodynamics as a better indicator of recent interactions. Statistical analysis of nearly 600 ME demonstrates that 45% exhibit net heating with a solar cycle dependence. Notably, High-impact ejecta preferentially exhibit stronger heating signatures, establishing thermal state as a complementary diagnostic of geoeffectiveness. Overall, this thesis establishes CMEs as intrinsically non-adiabatic systems whose thermodynamic evolution is coupled to expansion, internal force balance, solar-cycle variability, and CME-CME interactions, with important implications for understanding geoeffectiveness and improving space-weather assessment.

AI.tldr: This thesis builds a modeling-and-observational framework (FRIS) to constrain the thermodynamic evolution of CMEs, showing they are intrinsically non-adiabatic systems whose thermal state couples to expansion, internal force balance, solar-cycle variability, and CME-CME interactions, and that heating signatures serve as a complementary geoeffectiveness diagnostic.
AI.motivation: CMEs drive space weather, but their thermodynamic evolution is poorly constrained; in particular, fixed polytropic-index assumptions in MHD propagation models are unvalidated and internal plasma properties are largely inaccessible observationally.
AI.method: Develops the FRIS analytical model, which uses observed kinematics to infer internal plasma properties (e.g., the polytropic index); combines multi-viewpoint remote-sensing observations of fast CMEs with in situ measurements at 1 au; analyzes interacting CMEs from the May 2024 storm; and performs statistical analysis of ~600 magnetic ejecta (MEs) with solar-cycle considerations.
AI.result: Fast CMEs show an initial heat-release phase transitioning to near-isothermal evolution around 3-9 solar radii; thermal-pressure and centrifugal forces (opposed by Lorentz force) link expansion to thermal evolution, revealing limitations of a fixed polytropic index. At 1 au, persistent non-adiabatic evolution with turbulence and localized intermittency appears. Interacting May 2024 CMEs show restructured magnetic/thermal configurations, double-flux-rope-like signatures, and species-dependent heating, with electron thermodynamics a better indicator of recent interactions. Among ~600 MEs, 45% show net heating with solar-cycle dependence, and high-impact ejecta preferentially show stronger heating.
AI.conclusion: CMEs are intrinsically non-adiabatic systems whose thermodynamic evolution is coupled to expansion, internal force balance, solar-cycle variability, and CME-CME interactions; thermal state is a complementary diagnostic of geoeffectiveness with implications for space-weather assessment.

title: Probing the Assembly of Triangulum: Precision Metallicities and $α$ Abundances of M33's Star Clusters from APOGEE Integrated-Light Spectroscopy
comment: 29 pages, 16 figures
summary: The star cluster system of M33 provides an excellent opportunity to investigate whether galaxy formation physics is dependent on a galaxy's mass. Older globular clusters (GCs) trace hierarchical assembly and chemical enrichment, while younger clusters trace the recent star formation. By studying the M33 star cluster system as a whole, we can probe the formation physics of galaxies at a lower mass than the Milky Way, and look for signals of accretion. To that end, we present analysis of 37 M33 star clusters using high-resolution ($R\sim22,500$), near-infrared (1.5-1.7 $μ$m), integrated light spectra from the APOGEE survey. We use full-spectrum fitting to obtain precision measurements of the clusters' kinematics, metallicities, and $α$ abundances. We identify three populations of clusters from our measurements: young stellar clusters (~100 Myr) with broad Brackett absorption features; intermediate-age clusters (1-2 Gyr) that are metal-rich ([M/H]=-0.5 to +0.3) with roughly solar $α$ abundance; and old (>5 Gyr), kinematically-hot and metal-poor GCs. These old GCs exhibit a broad range of kinematics (RV~-250 to -8 km s$^{-1}$), metallicities ([M/H]=-1.8 to -0.6) and $α$ abundances ([$α$/M]=+0.05 to +0.3), and we identify and discuss three GCs that show strong chemodynamical evidence of accretion into M33's halo. M33's GCs at [M/H]~-1.2 have a spread in [$α$/M] of nearly 0.2 dex. This pattern is strikingly similar to the abundance distribution of Milky Way GCs, and indicates either that M33 and the Milky Way formed clusters similarly at early times, or that M33 hosts a significant population of accreted clusters in its halo.

AI.tldr: Full-spectrum fitting of 37 M33 star clusters from APOGEE near-IR spectra reveals three populations (young, intermediate-age, old), with three old GCs showing chemodynamical evidence of accretion and an [α/M] spread resembling the Milky Way's GC abundance distribution.
AI.motivation: The M33 star cluster system offers a chance to test whether galaxy formation physics depends on galaxy mass, probing lower-mass galaxy formation and accretion signatures than the Milky Way. Old GCs trace hierarchical assembly and chemical enrichment, while young clusters trace recent star formation.
AI.method: High-resolution (R~22,500) near-infrared (1.5-1.7 μm) integrated-light spectra of 37 M33 star clusters from APOGEE, analyzed with full-spectrum fitting to measure kinematics, metallicities, and α abundances.
AI.result: Three populations identified: young (~100 Myr) clusters with broad Brackett absorption; intermediate-age (1-2 Gyr) metal-rich clusters ([M/H]=-0.5 to +0.3) with roughly solar α; and old (>5 Gyr), kinematically hot, metal-poor GCs spanning RV~-250 to -8 km/s, [M/H]=-1.8 to -0.6, and [α/M]=+0.05 to +0.3. Three GCs show strong chemodynamical evidence of accretion into M33's halo; GCs at [M/H]~-1.2 show ~0.2 dex spread in [α/M], strikingly similar to the Milky Way GC abundance distribution.
AI.conclusion: The abundance pattern indicates either that M33 and the Milky Way formed clusters similarly at early times, or that M33 hosts a significant population of accreted clusters in its halo.

title: Linear Polarimetry of the Solar Corona during the Total Solar Eclipse of 8 April 2024: Multi-Band Observations and HDR Imaging
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures. Accepted in Solar Physics
summary: High-Dynamic-Range (HDR) multi-band linear polarimetry of the solar corona during total solar eclipses provides a vital ground-based diagnostic tool for mapping plasma morphology and magnetic topology in the inner and middle corona. Extracting reliable polarimetric signals requires rigorous observational calibration, spatial co-alignment, and noise reduction via stacking. We report optical linear polarimetric observations acquired during the 8 April 2024 total solar eclipse from Dallas, Texas, USA, near solar maximum. Using a full-frame color CMOS detector paired with an 80~mm refractor, multi-band Red, Green, and Blue (RGB) images were recorded simultaneously across three polarizer orientations ($-60^\circ$, $0^\circ$, and $+60^\circ$) using a 9-step exposure bracket ($1/800\text{~s}$ to $1/3\text{~s}$). We present an end-to-end data-reduction pipeline incorporating: (i)~a novel astrometric registration framework that reconstructs Sun-centric solar-disk coordinates via lunar-limb fitting, catalog star plate-solving, and ephemeris displacement calculations, achieving sub-pixel alignment; (ii)~a photometrically linear exposure-normalization HDR image synthesis; and (iii)~Multi-scale Gaussian Normalization (MGN) coupled with Polarization-to-RGB chromatic mapping. The resulting structurally enhanced polarization composites unravel a complex solar-maximum coronal topology characterized by helmet streamers and fine-scale striations traceable out to $\sim3\,R_\odot$. This framework establishes a high-resolution, photometrically calibrated dataset ready for subsequent polarized brightness ($pB$) and electron density inversions.

AI.tldr: The paper presents HDR multi-band linear polarimetric observations of the solar corona from the 8 April 2024 total solar eclipse (Dallas, USA), with an end-to-end data-reduction pipeline for astrometric registration, HDR synthesis, and enhanced polarization imaging.
AI.motivation: HDR multi-band linear polarimetry during total solar eclipses is a vital ground-based diagnostic for mapping plasma morphology and magnetic topology in the inner and middle corona, but extracting reliable polarimetric signals demands rigorous calibration, co-alignment, and noise reduction.
AI.method: RGB full-frame CMOS imaging with an 80 mm refractor across three polarizer orientations (−60°, 0°, +60°) using a 9-step exposure bracket (1/800 s to 1/3 s). The pipeline includes (i) an astrometric registration framework reconstructing Sun-centric solar-disk coordinates via lunar-limb fitting, catalog star plate-solving, and ephemeris displacement (sub-pixel alignment); (ii) photometrically linear exposure-normalization HDR synthesis; and (iii) Multi-scale Gaussian Normalization (MGN) with polarization-to-RGB chromatic mapping.
AI.result: Structurally enhanced polarization composites reveal complex solar-maximum coronal topology with helmet streamers and fine-scale striations traceable to ~3 R_sun, yielding a high-resolution, photometrically calibrated dataset.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a calibrated dataset ready for subsequent polarized brightness (pB) and electron density inversions.

title: Extending the M33 Extinction Map with Radio and Far-Infrared Gas Observations
summary: As the third-largest galaxy in the Local Group, M33 requires high-precision, wide-area extinction maps to recover the intrinsic luminosity and enable accurate studies, yet the available maps remain limited in coverage. In this work, we extend the stellar-based extinction map within the Panchromatic Hubble Andromeda Treasury: Triangulum Extended Region (PHATTER) footprint to the outer disk by calibrating empirical $A_V$-H\,\textsc{i} and $A_V$-total hydrogen relations in the PHATTER overlap region. Within the PHATTER footprint, we retain the stellar-based map at 6$^{\prime\prime}$ resolution, and outside the area covered by the stellar-based extinction map we produce an extended map at $\approx 12^{\prime\prime}$ resolution. The resulting map preserves a continuous morphology across the PHATTER boundary and reveals clear spiral-arm and interarm contrast and patchy dust substructures across a broader area. The median and maximum extinction values, $\mathrm{median}(A_V)\approx 0.91$ mag and $A_{V,\mathrm{max}} \approx 2.62$ mag, are consistent with the high-extinction range reported by previous M33 studies, while naturally reflecting differences in tracers and spatial coverage. The extinction map provides a practical, publicly available dataset for galaxy-wide extinction correction and for further studies in M33.

AI.tldr: This work extends the stellar-based extinction map of M33 beyond the PHATTER footprint by calibrating empirical A_V–HI and A_V–total hydrogen relations, yielding a continuous, wide-area map that reveals spiral-arm and dust substructure across the outer disk.
AI.motivation: M33, the third-largest Local Group galaxy, needs high-precision, wide-area extinction maps to recover intrinsic luminosity, but existing maps have limited coverage, especially outside the PHATTER region.
AI.method: Empirical A_V–H I and A_V–total hydrogen relations are calibrated in the PHATTER overlap region. The stellar-based map is retained at 6'' resolution inside the PHATTER footprint, and an extended map at ~12'' resolution is produced outside it using the calibrated gas-extinction relations.
AI.result: The extended map preserves continuous morphology across the PHATTER boundary and reveals clear spiral-arm/interarm contrast and patchy dust substructures over a broader area, with median(A_V) ≈ 0.91 mag and A_V,max ≈ 2.62 mag, consistent with previous high-extinction reports.
AI.conclusion: The authors provide a practical, publicly available wide-area extinction map for galaxy-wide extinction correction and further studies in M33, with differences from prior work attributed to tracers and spatial coverage.

title: Low-mass and High-sSFR H$α$ Emitters at $z \sim 2$ in the ZFOURGE-COSMOS Field
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We present a near-infrared spectroscopic follow-up study of seven H$α$ emitter candidates at $z\sim2$ in the ZFOURGE-COSMOS field, selected via the $K_{\rm s}$-band flux excess method. Spectra obtained with Subaru/SWIMS confirm strong H$α$ emission line at $z=2.06-2.49$ for all the targets. Three galaxies are low-mass systems ($\log(M_\star/M_\odot) < 9$) with high specific SFRs, while four are high-mass systems ($\log(M_\star/M_\odot) > 10$) on the star-forming main sequence. The low-mass galaxies show consistent H$α$ flux measurements between the $K_{\rm s}$-band flux excess method and the spectroscopy, whereas the high-mass galaxies show higher H$α$ flux inferred from the $K_{\rm s}$-band flux excess than the spectroscopic measurement which may be attributed to their extended star formation distributions. The low-mass galaxies exhibit extreme [O III] $\lambda5007$ emission with high rest-frame equivalent widths ($\mathrm{EW}_{\mathrm{rest}}$) ranging from 480 to 1064 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$. They are characterized by high [O III]/H$β$ ratios ($>4$) and weak [O II] and [N II] emission lines, indicating high ionization parameters and low metallicity. The line ratios are comparable to those of star-forming galaxies at $z \gtrsim 6$ and their local analogs. JWST/NIRCam imaging reveals a clear mass-dependent color gradient: the low-mass galaxies present positive F115W-F277W radial gradients with blue cores, while the high-mass galaxies exhibit negative gradients with red cores. These results suggest distinct assembly pathways for low- and high-mass galaxies during the cosmic noon epoch.

AI.tldr: Near-IR spectroscopy with Subaru/SWIMS confirms seven z~2 H-alpha emitters selected by Ks-band flux excess; low-mass galaxies show extreme [O III] emission and blue cores, high-mass ones show red cores, indicating distinct assembly pathways.
AI.motivation: The Ks-band flux excess method is used to select H-alpha emitter candidates at z~2, but spectroscopic confirmation and characterization of these candidates—and how their properties depend on stellar mass—remain needed.
AI.method: Subaru/SWIMS near-infrared spectroscopy of seven H-alpha emitter candidates at z~2 in the ZFOURGE-COSMOS field selected via Ks-band flux excess; comparison of H-alpha fluxes between selection method and spectroscopy; measurement of [O III], H-beta, [O II], [N II] line ratios and rest-frame EWs; JWST/NIRCam F115W-F277W radial color gradients.
AI.result: All seven targets show strong H-alpha at z=2.06-2.49. Three low-mass (log M*/Msun<9) high-sSFR systems; four high-mass (log M*/Msun>10) main-sequence systems. Low-mass galaxies have consistent H-alpha fluxes between methods; high-mass show higher Ks-inferred H-alpha, possibly from extended star formation. Low-mass galaxies show extreme [O III] lambda5007 with EW_rest=480-1064 Angstrom, [O III]/H-beta>4, weak [O II] and [N II], indicating high ionization parameter and low metallicity, similar to z>6 star-forming galaxies and local analogs. NIRCam imaging shows mass-dependent color gradients: positive F115W-F277W gradients with blue cores for low-mass, negative gradients with red cores for high-mass.
AI.conclusion: Low- and high-mass galaxies at z~2 exhibit distinct properties in H-alpha flux consistency, ionization/metallicity, and radial color gradients, suggesting different assembly pathways during cosmic noon.
